what_this_is: The game's history knowledge base: people, expeditions, dated events, place-name origins and short fact cards keyed to park node ids. Much of it rests on the work of Robert L. Wood (1925-2003), the historian of how the Olympic Mountains were explored, whose facts are retold here in our own words and credited. No sentence of Wood's appears in this file. Verbatim lines from public-domain sources live in quotes_public_domain.json and are linked here by quote id.

fact_cards.title: Our Lady of the Angels
fact_cards.text: The harbor got its name from a Spanish ship. In 1791 Francisco de Eliza called it the Port of Our Lady of the Angels. Later Spanish and British chart-makers trimmed the name, and Vancouver's short form, Port Angeles, stuck. Mount Angeles and Lake Angeles probably took the name from the town. Long before any chart, this shore was the homeland of the Klallam people, and it still is.
fact_cards.look: You see the harbor town at the foot of the mountains. A Spanish captain named this harbor for Our Lady of the Angels in 1791.

fact_cards.title: South from Port Angeles, 1885
fact_cards.text: On July 17, 1885, Lt. Joseph O'Neil led a small Army party south out of Port Angeles with a string of pack mules. The town then had about forty people, a hotel, a sawmill and two stores. Their guide left them on the first night. For about a month the men cut a mule trail up through the foothills toward the high ridges, working six in the morning to six at night on bacon, beans, flour and coffee.
fact_cards.look: You see the foothills rising behind the town. An Army party cut a mule trail up into them in July 1885.

fact_cards.title: The schoolchildren's sign
fact_cards.text: On September 30, 1937, President Franklin Roosevelt came through Port Angeles. Schoolchildren held up a sign asking for a national park, and he gave his first firm promise. The next day he toured the loop road through Forks and past Lake Quinault. Congress created Olympic National Park on June 29, 1938. Its first superintendent, Preston Macy, ran it at first from the attic of his Port Angeles house.
fact_cards.look: You see the visitor center. The park it serves was created in 1938, a year after a president passed through this town.
fact_cards.ranger_line: The park's first superintendent ran it from his attic, down the road. We have more room now. Not much more.

fact_cards.title: A lieutenant's idea
fact_cards.text: In November 1890, after two expeditions, Lt. O'Neil wrote his report. The outer slopes held fine timber, he said, but the high interior was no good for farms or mines. It would, however, make a fine national park, chiefly to save the elk. He said the same in a Portland lecture that December. Congress made the park in June 1938, forty-eight years on. O'Neil, risen by then to general, died about a month later.

fact_cards.title: The man who wrote it down
fact_cards.text: Much of what this book knows about the park's past comes from Robert L. Wood (1925-2003). He first saw the Olympics in 1946 and spent about half a century walking, climbing and reading about them. He earned his living as a court shorthand reporter. He wrote the histories of the Press and O'Neil expeditions and the standard guide to the Olympic trails. His papers are at the University of Washington.
fact_cards.look: You see a shelf of six worn books behind the counter. They are all by the same man.
fact_cards.ranger_line: Most of what I know about who came first, I got off that shelf. Robert Wood. Read him on a rest day.

fact_cards.title: Heart O' the Hills
fact_cards.text: The name came from a small roadside resort on the north side of Mount Angeles, open from the late 1920s, with a store, a gas pump and cabins. In 1933 young men of the Civilian Conservation Corps, based at their camp on the Elwha, built road toward here. Much earlier, in July 1885, Lt. O'Neil's mule trail climbed through these same foothills toward the ridges above.
fact_cards.look: You see the campground among big trees. The name came from a little roadside resort of the 1920s.

fact_cards.title: Named for the wind
fact_cards.text: An Elwha settler wrote to the historian Edmond Meany that Hurricane Hill was probably named for the speed of the winds up here at times. Nobody recorded who said it first. In August 1885 Lt. O'Neil's party came along this ridge and split up. One group, under the engineer Harry Hawgood, headed down toward the Elwha, lost its supplies in a river crossing and turned back.
fact_cards.look: You see grass flattened in one direction. The settlers who named this hill thought about the wind too.

fact_cards.title: Mount Sherman, briefly
fact_cards.text: In July 1885 Lt. O'Neil's men cut their mule trail toward a peak he called Mount Sherman. They crossed the first ridge by a pass near it, which he called Victors Pass. By 1890 the people of Port Angeles had already renamed the peak Mount Angeles. Near here O'Neil saw his compass needle swing, pulled aside, he thought, by a body of magnetic iron in the rock.
fact_cards.look: You see Mount Angeles. In 1885 an Army lieutenant called it Mount Sherman. The name lasted about five years.

fact_cards.title: The Sisters
fact_cards.text: O'Neil called these heights, Mount Angeles and Klahhane Ridge, The Sisters. From up here in 1885 he looked south over a wild jumble of peaks and picked out one cluster as Mount Olympus. Klahhane comes from a Chinook Jargon word meaning out of doors. A Port Angeles hiking club was using the name by 1918. Whether the club named the ridge is not known.
fact_cards.look: You see a jumble of peaks to the south. In 1885 a lieutenant stood up here and guessed which one was Olympus.

fact_cards.title: Along the ridges, 1885
fact_cards.text: From Hurricane Ridge in August 1885, O'Neil's main group followed the open ridges south and east, on much the same line as today's trail from Obstruction Point. Up here the brush thinned out and the going got easier. Elk and deer were everywhere. The mules still had to be coaxed along the steep sidehills, and more than one of them went tumbling down the slope.
fact_cards.look: You see open ridges running south. An Army mule train came along here in August 1885.

fact_cards.title: Noplace
fact_cards.text: O'Neil's mules went no farther than a camp he named Noplace, probably here in Cameron Basin. He wrote that his trail led from Port Angeles to Noplace, in the heart of the mountains. From here he and Private John Johnson set off on foot toward the Mount Anderson country. They became separated, and Johnson walked out alone. Then a courier came with new orders, and the trip was over.
fact_cards.look: You see a wide green basin under the peaks. In 1885 an Army lieutenant named his camp here Noplace.

fact_cards.title: Claywood, Fromme and Hayden
fact_cards.text: Mount Claywood, above these meadows, carries the name of H. Clay Wood, the Army officer who signed O'Neil's orders in 1885. In 1920 a party of Mountaineers climbed it and went on to a peak about a mile northwest, which they named Mount Fromme for the forest supervisor who was with them. By then Hayden Pass already had its name. Who Hayden was is not recorded in the sources behind this book.

fact_cards.title: The governor's dare
fact_cards.text: In the fall of 1889 Elisha Ferry, soon to be the new state's first governor, called the Olympic interior an unknown land. It was unknown only to newcomers; the peninsula's tribes knew it well. The Seattle Press dared someone to cross it. James Christie, a Scot who had spent three years on an Arctic expedition, offered to lead. Six men left in December with four dogs, two mules and about 1,500 pounds of gear, planning to be deep in the range by spring.

fact_cards.title: A quarter of a mile
fact_cards.text: The Press party tried to haul its supplies up the winter Elwha in a leaky flat-bottomed boat named Gertie, pulling her on a towline. On January 14, 1890, they gained about a quarter of a mile. They stood in the river to their belts, among floating ice, and afterward the air read 16 degrees. Charles Barnes wrote it all down that night. After ten or twelve days and only a few miles, they left Gertie on the bank.
fact_cards.look: You see the Elwha, quick and green and cold. In January 1890 six men dragged a boat up it, a quarter mile a day.
fact_cards.ranger_line: In January 1890 some men hauled a boat up this river in their shirtsleeves, more or less. Wear more than they did.

fact_cards.title: The river let go
fact_cards.text: In 1910 work began on a dam across the lower Elwha, and in 1927 a second dam rose at Glines Canyon. Neither had a way for fish to pass, so salmon that once ran deep into the mountains stopped about five miles from the sea. The reservoirs flooded Klallam homeland. After a long campaign led by the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, removal began in September 2011. By 2014 both dams were gone, and the salmon came back up.
fact_cards.look: You see the spillway where a dam stood until 2014. Below it the river runs to the sea again.
fact_cards.ranger_line: This was a lake when I started. Now it's a river with salmon in it. The Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe worked a long time for that.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: National Park Service; Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe.

fact_cards.title: Fifty pounds of fireworks
fact_cards.text: The Press party packed fifty pounds of colored fire, meant to be set off on a peak where Seattle could see it. It rode on the mule Jennie. On a steep ridge the men called the Devil's Backbone, somewhere above the old Elwha ranger station, Jennie slipped and fell to her death. The fireworks went with her. Seattle never saw its signal, and the men carried her load on their own backs.

fact_cards.title: Camp Elwha
fact_cards.text: In June 1933 the Civilian Conservation Corps set up Camp Elwha near the old ranger station. By mid-July its young men had barracks, a mess hall and a bathhouse, and road crews had built a mile and a half of road toward Glines Canyon. They built trails, campgrounds at Whiskey Bend and Lake Mills, and kitchens that still stand. Other camps on the peninsula included Slab Camp, Quilcene and Lake Cushman.
fact_cards.look: You see an old log kitchen shelter. Young men of the Civilian Conservation Corps built it in the 1930s.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983).

flags.check: 'Kitchens that still stand': Evans says the Elwha and Altaire community kitchens survive (1983); confirm their condition today before using the Look line.

fact_cards.title: One more trip back
fact_cards.text: From late January to April 1890 the Press party moved up the Elwha like a slow tide. They carried about forty 50-pound packs forward by snowshoe and sled, then walked back for more, so each stretch was walked many times over. Some days the whole camp moved a mile and a half. By late February half the food was gone, and beyond the canyon nobody in the settlements could tell them anything about the way ahead.

fact_cards.title: The Goblin Gates
fact_cards.text: Here the whole Elwha squeezes through a slot of rock about twelve feet wide. In March 1890 Charles Barnes of the Press party looked at the walls and saw faces in them, so he named the place the Goblin Gates. Today's signs say Goblins Gate. Nearby, James Christie caught fourteen trout in half an hour, and the deer showed no fear of the men. Robert L. Wood later wrote an article called 'The Goblin Gates Refound.'
fact_cards.look: You see the river pour through a gap of rock not much wider than a road. In 1890 a man saw goblin faces in these walls.

fact_cards.title: The geysers that weren't
fact_cards.text: In March 1890 the Press party camped in this valley and heard something strange. A thumping began slowly, sped up until the beats ran together, and stopped. It came again and again. They decided it must be hidden geysers, and the valley has been Geyser Valley ever since. A rival party heard nothing that summer, and nobody has found a geyser here yet. The sound fits a ruffed grouse drumming in spring.
fact_cards.look: You hear, or think you hear, a soft drumming in the woods. In 1890 men decided it was a geyser.

fact_cards.title: The Humes brothers
fact_cards.text: Will Humes came west in 1897 from a New York farm family that guided hunters in the Adirondacks. He was looking for gold. His brother Grant followed in 1899. They stayed to hunt, farm and pack, and about 1900 they built this log cabin. In 1907 they packed for climbers, including The Mountaineers' first outing. Will went back east about 1916. Grant stayed on the Elwha until his last illness, and died in 1934.
fact_cards.look: You see a log cabin in a meadow above the river. Two brothers from New York built it about 1900.
fact_cards.ranger_line: The Humes brothers packed for every climbing party that came up this valley in 1907. Their cabin is still standing. Be nice to it.

fact_cards.title: Krause Bottom
fact_cards.text: This flat carries the name of Ernst Krause, a German-born painter from Tacoma, and his wife, Meta. They homesteaded here in the 1890s, clearing the bottomland by burning slash, the usual way then. One of their fires got away from them. It burned their buildings and their animals. The Krauses' name stayed on the flat after they had gone.
fact_cards.look: You see a quiet flat by the river. A painter and his wife homesteaded here in the 1890s.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983).

fact_cards.title: Cougar Mike
fact_cards.text: E. O. Michael, known as Cougar Mike, came to the Elwha probably in the 1920s. He hunted cougars for the bounty, trapped, packed mules for the Forest Service and later built trails for the Park Service. About 1937 he built this small cabin with two friends, Jay Gormley and Gus Peterson. It still stands beside the trail.

fact_cards.title: Older blazes than theirs
fact_cards.text: Between Geyser Valley and the Lillian River, the Press party marked its way with three blazes, one above another, cut into the trees. Then they found blazes far older than their own, healed over inside living trees. One old cut had about 210 growth rings over it. They also found old posts used for working hides. People had travelled this valley long before 1890.

fact_cards.title: April 1, 1890
fact_cards.text: On April 1, 1890, the Press party reached this side stream and named it the Lillian River. Nobody wrote down who Lillian was. At the far end of the valley they would name two lakes Mary and Margaret, also without saying why. They had been on the Elwha almost four months. The divide was still more than a month away.
fact_cards.look: You see the Lillian River joining the Elwha. Nobody wrote down who Lillian was.

fact_cards.title: Doc Ludden's roadhouse
fact_cards.text: About 1906 a retired Tacoma policeman named A. Ludden, called Doc, settled just below Humes Ranch. He kept bees and sealed his honey in milk tins. He used old photographic plates for window glass. Tin-can signs along the trail offered meals, beds, honey, haircuts and root beer. He stayed about twenty years. Ludden Peak, up here, carries his name.
fact_cards.look: You see Ludden Peak. It is named for a beekeeper who sold root beer and haircuts on the Elwha trail.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983).

fact_cards.title: The lookout on Dodger Point
fact_cards.text: The Forest Service built this fifteen-foot-square lookout in 1933, perhaps with help from the Civilian Conservation Corps. Its first lookout was a man called Dodger Bender, and the point is said to be named for him. In the winter of 1942-43 it became a post of the Aircraft Warning Service, watching the sky for enemy planes. It is one of the few lookouts left in the park.
fact_cards.look: You see a small square lookout with windows on every side. In the winter of 1942 someone watched the sky from it all day.

fact_cards.title: Elkhorn
fact_cards.text: This was already Elkhorn Flat in 1907, when The Mountaineers planned their third camp here on the way up the Elwha. The Forest Service built the four log buildings of the guard station between 1930 and 1934, about eleven and a half miles from Whiskey Bend. In April 1890 the Press party had come through this stretch, the wide upper valley they called Press Valley, in snow up to their waists.
fact_cards.look: You see a log guard station in a wide flat. The Forest Service built it in the early 1930s.

fact_cards.title: The youngest man
fact_cards.text: The Hayes River is named for Christopher Hayes, a cowboy from the Yakima Valley and, at twenty-two, the youngest of the Press party. The river joins the Elwha in the long upper valley the party called Press Valley. Somewhere along here, in April 1890, a bull elk kicked one of their dogs, Dike, and killed him. The other dogs went on to save the men from starving at the divide.
fact_cards.look: You see the Hayes River meet the Elwha. It is named for a twenty-two-year-old cowboy who walked across these mountains in 1890.
fact_cards.ranger_line: Elk look calm until they don't. One killed the Press party's dog near here in 1890. Give them fifty yards, half a football field.

fact_cards.title: The wrong way up the Goldie
fact_cards.text: In April 1890 the Press party saw a gap leading off the Elwha and took it for the way south. It was the Goldie River, steep and trackless. They spent days climbing out through deep snow with heavy packs. The worn-out mule Dollie lay down and would not rise, so they took off her halter and set her free. Later their own trail notes told others to keep to the main valley instead.

fact_cards.title: Elk Lick
fact_cards.text: Frederick Remann, a Tacoma lawyer and later a Pierce County judge, fished the Elwha for years. In the 1920s he had this cabin built, with Grant Humes overseeing the work, and called it Elk Lick. About 1939 the river changed course and crowded the cabin, so it was taken apart and rebuilt on the higher shelf where it stands now. Remann came to fish almost until his death in 1949.
fact_cards.look: You see a log cabin on a shelf above the river. It was moved up here, log by log, when the Elwha changed its mind.

fact_cards.title: Three summits in a day
fact_cards.text: The patrol cabin near Camp Wilder began as the fishing cabin of H. H. Botten in the 1920s. Botten was one of four Bremerton men who, on July 7, 1908, climbed all three summits of Mount Olympus in a single day. The peak above, now Mount Wilder, is thought to be the one the Press party named Mount Barnes in 1890. The name Barnes later moved to another peak.

fact_cards.title: Chicago Camp
fact_cards.text: By August 1905 this spot already had its name, when Grant Humes used Chicago Camp as his base, ten miles below the source of the Elwha. The records do not say where the name came from. In 1900 a scientific party from Chicago's Field Columbian Museum worked in the Elwha, and the camp may be named for them. In May 1890 the Press party had passed this way, climbing toward the divide.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: The Mountaineer, 1907; Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983); Peninsula Daily News.
fact_cards.confidence: low for the naming idea; high that the name existed by 1905

fact_cards.title: Sixty-five Mountaineers
fact_cards.text: In the summer of 1907 a young Seattle club called The Mountaineers chose the Olympics for its first annual outing. Port Angeles cut trail up the Elwha for them. Sixty-five people walked in, twenty-six of them women, and set up their main camp here in the Elwha Basin. Women climbed in bloomers or knickerbockers. No guns were allowed. Every boot needed hobnails and spare calks.
fact_cards.look: You see the head of the Elwha valley. In 1907 sixty-five climbers camped here, in hobnailed boots.

fact_cards.title: Water running south
fact_cards.text: On May 5, 1890, the Press party came up between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and named two small lakes, Mary and Margaret. At first they took the ground between the lakes for the divide. The true pass lay just beyond, a low saddle they called Elwha Pass. By a big rock, a hole in the snow showed water running south, away from the Elwha. They were over the top. Today the saddle is Low Divide.
fact_cards.look: You see a low saddle between two big mountains. Here, in May 1890, five tired men found water running the other way.
fact_cards.ranger_line: Low Divide. The Press party crossed it in May 1890 and named it Elwha Pass. Nobody calls it that now. The name didn't take; they did.

fact_cards.title: Three bears
fact_cards.text: By the time the Press party crossed the divide, the dogs had eaten the last of the bacon, and the men were down to flour soup. Just past the pass the dogs brought three bears to bay. The meat kept the party from starving, and the men drank the grease straight from the pan. A month after the crossing, Christie took two of the dogs north with him to Alaska.

fact_cards.title: The chalet at Low Divide
fact_cards.text: In 1926 a Grays Harbor company got a permit to build a log chalet here, to sell the wilderness to visitors without a road through it. The main chalet, thirty-five by fifty feet, was finished in 1927, with a bathhouse and cabins after. There was talk of an airstrip, a lake for seaplanes and a tram up a nearby mountain. None was built. An avalanche took the chalet in the winter of 1944.
fact_cards.look: You see a meadow with nothing in it. A log chalet stood here until an avalanche took it in 1944.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983).

fact_cards.title: The ice tunnel
fact_cards.text: At the head of the Elwha a long tongue of old snow fills the canyon. In 1896 S. C. Gilman described an ice tunnel here, twenty feet high and forty wide in summer, running two and a half miles under the ice. Those were his figures. In 1905 Grant Humes wrote that the thought of falling in was enough to make anyone crawl. By August 1920 climbers found the snowfinger growing dangerous to cross.
fact_cards.look: You see a long tongue of gray snow in the canyon. Somewhere underneath it, water is talking.
fact_cards.ranger_line: The snowfinger gets thin from below, where you can't see it. By August, people go around.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: S. C. Gilman, National Geographic, 1896; The Mountaineer, 1907; The Mountaineer, 1920.

flags.hazard_card: Use before the snowfinger as foreshadowing, never on a death page.

fact_cards.title: The baking-powder can
fact_cards.text: On August 12, 1907, three Mountaineers found a one-pound baking-powder can on a knoll at this pass. Inside were notes. The oldest, dated August 25, 1894, had been left by three men on their way to the Pacific from Port Townsend. Others had added notes in 1900. That July a New York climbing party had named the pass for Arthur Dodwell and Theodore Rixon, whose survey crews mapped the range in 1898-1900.
fact_cards.look: You see a knoll on the pass. In 1907 climbers found a tin can here full of other people's notes.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: The Mountaineer, 1907; Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983); USGS Professional Paper 7 (1902).

fact_cards.title: The Garden of the Gods
fact_cards.text: In September 1890 a small party from O'Neil's expedition, led by Nelson Linsley, climbed a long glacier to the head of the Queets. They crossed a gulch they called Pluto's Gulch and came out on a high plateau full of flowers. The naturalist, Bernard Bretherton, called it an inspiration and named it the Garden of the Gods. Exactly where it was is not certain. This basin may be the place.
fact_cards.look: You see a high basin full of flowers. In 1890 a naturalist called a place like this the Garden of the Gods.

fact_cards.title: Turned back by the wind
fact_cards.text: On August 10, 1907, The Mountaineers' first try for Olympus set out from a camp in the upper Queets. A gale of about thirty miles an hour drove them back. On the wet heather one climber, Winona Bailey, fell about a hundred feet. A doctor in the party dressed her wounds, and she was cared for over several days at a spot they named Hospital Camp. She recovered, and in 1920 she wrote the account of the club's next big outing.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: The Mountaineer, 1907; The Mountaineer, 1920.

flags.note: A real person's fall that she survived. Use on camp-reading or survived-fall pages only, never on a death page.

fact_cards.title: A range named for a newspaper owner
fact_cards.text: On April 27, 1890, the Press party named this long line of peaks the Bailey Range, for William E. Bailey, who owned the Seattle Press. Many of its peaks carry the names of 1890 newspapermen and patrons. Some names wandered. The peak the party called Mount Ferry, for the governor, is the one people now call Mount Pulitzer, and the name Ferry moved to the next peak northeast.
fact_cards.look: You see the Bailey Range, white and jagged. Most of its peaks are named for newspapermen of 1890.

fact_cards.title: Bob Wood's August
fact_cards.text: In August 1961 three climbers, Bob Wood, Doug Waali and Kent Heathershaw, made what were reported as first ascents of three Bailey Range peaks. They climbed Mount Childs on August 6, then Mount Pulitzer, and on August 8 Stephen Peak, from the upper Cream Lake basin. Childs and Pulitzer carry Press Expedition names that never became official. This Bob Wood was very probably Robert L. Wood, the historian behind this book's history.
fact_cards.look: You see Stephen Peak above the basin. A man who later wrote this park's history probably stood on it in 1961.

fact_cards.title: Olympic Hot Springs
fact_cards.text: Andrew Jacobsen reported warm springs on Boulder Creek in the early 1890s. Billy Everett found them again about 1907, and in 1909 they opened to the public. A lodge, a pool and cabins followed. A road arrived in 1930, and taxis ran from Port Angeles for $3.75. The hotel burned in 1940. The Park Service closed the resort in 1966 and took its buildings away in 1972 and 1973.
fact_cards.look: You see warm water seeping out of the bank. A hotel stood near here once. Now there is steam and moss.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983).

fact_cards.title: The Elwha
fact_cards.text: The British surveyor Henry Kellett put the name Elwha on a chart in 1847. In 1892 a missionary reported that the word meant elk, and the 1890 Press party said the same. Those were outsiders' readings. The valley is the homeland of the Klallam people, today the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, who have their own names for the river and its places.

fact_cards.title: A grand hotel in the woods
fact_cards.text: Theodor Moritz, a settler from the Quillayute River, claimed these springs before 1900, and sick people walked in to soak in tubs made of dugout logs. A lumberman, Michael Earles, believed the water had cured him. He built a road in from Lake Crescent and opened a hotel here on May 15, 1912, with 165 rooms, telephones, golf and a sanitarium with an X-ray machine. Four years later a faulty chimney flue started a fire that burned almost all of it.
fact_cards.look: You see steam over the pools. In 1912 a hotel with 165 rooms stood here. It lasted four years.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983).

flags.business_name_caution: Talks about the 1912 hotel only. The present-day resort appears in the game under its fictional name; do not name the real concession.

fact_cards.title: Soleduck or Sol Duc
fact_cards.text: Early maps counted this river as part of the Quillayute. By 1923 the springs were spelled Sol Duc and the river Soleduck, and both spellings are still in use. The hot-springs company told the historian Edmond Meany that the name meant magic waters. Like other meanings in old books, that one has not been confirmed by the tribes. The log buildings of the Eagle ranger station date from the Forest Service years of the 1930s.

fact_cards.title: Chris Morgenroth
fact_cards.text: This lake very probably carries the name of Chris Morgenroth. He came from Germany, homesteaded on the Bogachiel, and went to work as a ranger for the forest reserve in 1903. He built trails in the upper Bogachiel and the Hoh and around Lake Crescent. After the great Sol Duc fire of 1907 he led the replanting of a burn of 13,000 acres. In the 1930s he spoke up for a national park.
fact_cards.look: You see a small lake that most people never find. It probably carries the name of a ranger who planted a burned forest.

fact_cards.title: Storm King Ranger Station
fact_cards.text: The little ranger station by the Marymere Falls trail was built about 1905. It is one of the oldest Forest Service buildings on the peninsula, and it is tied to Chris Morgenroth, one of the first rangers here. In the 1980s it was moved about 250 feet from where it first stood. In 1915 a county ferry on the lake was christened the Storm King. Where the mountain's own name came from is not recorded.
fact_cards.look: You see a small log ranger station, about as old as the Forest Service.

fact_cards.title: Marymere
fact_cards.text: In 1906 the first resort hotel on Barnes Point opened under the name Marymere. Rose Littleton ran it with her assistant, Mary Daum. In 1914 the two of them opened another resort and named it Rosemary, from both their names. The waterfall up Barnes Creek shares the Marymere name, though who first gave it to the falls is not recorded.
fact_cards.look: You see a tall, thin waterfall. It shares its name with a lakeside hotel of 1906.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983).

fact_cards.title: The other Barnes
fact_cards.text: Barnes Point and Barnes Creek are named for Sarah Barnes and her son Paul, who staked a claim near the creek's mouth about 1890. They were not the family of Charles Barnes of the Press Expedition, as far as the records show, though his brother Pierre also took up a claim near the lake that year. Charles drew the first published map of Lake Crescent. Before the road, lodge guests were met at East Beach and brought across by launch.
fact_cards.look: You see a wooded point on the lake. It is named for a mother and son who claimed land here about 1890.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983); Seattle Post-Intelligencer, 1890.
fact_cards.confidence: medium (whether the two Barnes families were related is not known)

fact_cards.title: Lake Crescent
fact_cards.text: Before 1890 this was Lake Everett, or just Big Lake. Then boosters of Port Crescent, a townsite seven miles away on the strait, and the editor of its newspaper pushed the name Lake Crescent, and it stuck. In 1895 Admiral L. A. Beardslee caught about sixty pounds of big blue-backed trout here, and the scientist David Starr Jordan named them Beardslee trout. The lake has drawn anglers ever since.
fact_cards.look: You see deep blue water, very clear. It was called Big Lake before a newspaper renamed it.

fact_cards.title: A president at the lake
fact_cards.text: On the night of September 30, 1937, President Franklin Roosevelt stayed at a lodge on this lake. The next day he toured the loop road through Forks and past Lake Quinault, and he talked over where a new park's boundaries should run. Nine months later Congress created Olympic National Park. In 1946 the park was dedicated at another lakeside inn, the Rosemary.

fact_cards.title: The railroad that missed its war
fact_cards.text: In 1918 the Army needed Sitka spruce for airplane frames. Soldiers and civilians, up to 8,000 men, built a railroad thirty-six miles west from near Port Angeles, blasting along this shore of Lake Crescent and boring the line's only two tunnels here. It cost nearly $30,000 a mile. The last rail went down in late November 1918, after the war had ended. It never hauled a log for the war.
fact_cards.look: You see an old railroad tunnel in the rock above the water. The line was finished about three weeks too late.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983); USGS Professional Paper 7 (1902).
fact_cards.confidence: high that it missed the war; the exact finishing date varies by source

fact_cards.title: Steamers on the lake
fact_cards.text: Before roads ringed it, people crossed Lake Crescent by boat. The steamer Lady of the Lake ran between Piedmont on the north shore and Fairholm at the west end. Both places were named in 1893: Piedmont for its spot at the foot of a mountain, Fairholm by Mrs. George Machelle. That year two men built a faster steamer called The Flyer. In 1914 and 1915 the county launched two ferries at Piedmont, the Majority and the Storm King.

fact_cards.title: The Iron Man of the Hoh
fact_cards.text: John Huelsdonk came from Germany and settled on the upper Hoh about 1891, in a valley reached only by canoe and trail. In 1892 he brought his wife, Dora. He logged, packed for surveyors and hunters, built trails, and kept the Spruce post office in his home for twenty-nine years. Neighbors called him the Iron Man of the Hoh. The story of him carrying a cookstove with a sack of flour inside grew heavier with every telling.
fact_cards.look: You see a spruce as wide as a doorway, mossy to the elbows. A man once carried a whole cookstove up this valley, they say.
fact_cards.ranger_line: Huelsdonk packed a cookstove up this valley on his back. Or so they say. Your pack is lighter. Probably.

fact_cards.title: Where it began for Wood
fact_cards.text: In the spring of 1948 a University of Washington student wrote a term paper on the Olympic rain forest. The student was Robert L. Wood, and he later called that paper the seed of all his books. Others had noticed the forest first. In 1896 S. C. Gilman wrote that this was a great country for moss. In 1902 the government's timber surveyors said that underbrush grows best in dampness and gloom.
fact_cards.look: You see moss on everything, including other moss. A writer started his life's work with a school paper about this forest.

fact_cards.title: Olympus Guard Station
fact_cards.text: The Forest Service built the guard station here about 1935, when this valley was still national forest. A newspaper column says Huelsdonk's son-in-law, Charly Lewis, was the first Forest Service ranger posted on the upper Hoh, in 1919. Lewis Meadow, nearby, may carry his name. In 1978 a falling tree flattened the station's first shelter. Old trees here keep their own schedule.

fact_cards.title: Santa Rosalia
fact_cards.text: In 1774 the Spanish captain Juan Perez sailed past and named the great snowy mountain Santa Rosalia. On July 4, 1788, the British trader John Meares saw it and called it Mount Olympus, after the home of the Greek gods. Captain Vancouver kept that name on his chart in 1792, and in time the whole range became the Olympic Mountains. The peoples of this coast had their own names for it long before.

fact_cards.title: August 13, 1907
fact_cards.text: The West Peak, the true summit of Olympus, was first climbed on August 13, 1907, by eleven members of The Mountaineers led by L. A. Nelson. Anna Hubert was the first woman on top. They cheered, sang and built a cairn. In the record box they left a ten-cent piece, a bread ticket, a safety pin, a hairpin and two matches. Two days later Cora Smith Eaton became the first woman on the East Peak.
fact_cards.look: You see the top of Mount Olympus. Eleven people first stood here on August 13, 1907, and left two matches in a box.

fact_cards.title: Which summit was which
fact_cards.text: Olympus has three main summits, and its early climbers kept losing track of them. Jack McGlone, a packer for the government survey, reached the East Peak on August 12, 1899, and left a Shelton newspaper. The Mountaineers found it on August 12, 1907, eight years to the day. In 1908 four Bremerton men climbed one of the Five Fingers in cloud, sure it was the West Peak. Then they climbed all three real summits the same day.
fact_cards.look: You see a summit that looks like the top. Climbers in cloud have been fooled here since 1908.
fact_cards.ranger_line: In 1908 four men climbed the wrong peak in a cloud and called it the summit. Then they did the right ones. If it's socked in, wait.

fact_cards.title: A monument for the elk

On March 2, two days before he left office, President Theodore Roosevelt proclaimed Mount Olympus National Monument, to protect its glaciers and the summer range of the elk whose scientific name already honored him. A congressman had asked for it mainly for the elk, and Roosevelt told him to write it up and he would sign. Hunting in the monument ended in 1927.
fact_cards.look: You see elk tracks in the mud. In 1909 a president set this country aside partly for them.

Native canoeists took them about ten miles up the Queets, and Banta liked the bottomland eight miles up. Back in Tacoma they sold a plan: fifty dollars to be guided in and shown a claim. By spring 1890 thirty-one claims were staked, and more settlers came by steamer in 1891.

fact_cards.title: Down the Queets to the sea
fact_cards.text: In September 1890 Private Harry Fisher of O'Neil's expedition lost his party in an alder thicket below Olympus. That night they saw his fire far below, but he could not rejoin them. He gave up and followed the Queets down to the ocean, with help from Native people on the lower river. His companions, short of boots and food, came down the Queets too, instead of exploring the Hoh as ordered.

The Hoh Tribe calls itself Chala-at, People of the Hoh River, and it still lives on its reservation at the river's mouth.

fact_cards.title: Quileute country
fact_cards.text: This coast is the homeland of the Quileute people, who say their land once reached from these beaches up the rain-forest rivers to the glaciers of Mount Olympus. Their language is not known to be related to any other. In 1889 a one-square-mile reservation was set aside at La Push. That same year a settler who claimed the land burned all twenty-six houses in the village. The Quileute Tribe lives at La Push today.

fact_cards.title: Too much mail for Boston

By 1898 the postmaster, Kron Erickson, had renamed it Mora, after his home parish in Sweden. The name stayed by the river, on the campground and the ranger station.

The Park Service changed its name from the Swedish to the Norwegian Memorial in 1956.

fact_cards.title: Farthest west
fact_cards.text: In 1923 the historian Edmond Meany noted that Cape Alava is the farthest west point of the United States mainland south of Alaska. Up the coast, Captain Vancouver in 1792 put the name Flattery Rocks on the rocks south of Cape Flattery, guessing that was where Captain Cook had meant in 1778.

fact_cards.title: Ahlstrom's Prairie
fact_cards.text: About 1900 two Swedish-born homesteaders, Lars Ahlstrom and Peter Roose, took up neighboring claims on the wet, open prairies west of Lake Ozette. They kept sheep and gardens and took outside work for cash. By 1916 Roose had eighty to a hundred sheep. Later he sawed his own lumber with a converted Model A engine. They stayed for decades, and the prairie keeps Ahlstrom's name.

fact_cards.title: The Fourth of July, 1890
fact_cards.text: O'Neil's expedition landed at Lilliwaup on Hood Canal on July 2, 1890. There was no dock, so the mules were pushed off the steamer's deck to swim ashore. The trail to Lake Cushman, promised as good and six miles long, turned out steep, wet and choked with fallen trees. On the Fourth of July the men had a day off. The botanist, Louis Henderson, caught about a hundred trout.

fact_cards.title: Hood Canal to the Pacific, 1890
fact_cards.text: In the summer of 1890 Lt. Joseph O'Neil led a joint expedition of the Army and the Oregon Alpine Club across the range from east to west. Soldiers cut a mule trail of about 93 miles from Hood Canal, up the North Fork Skokomish, over the divides and down the Quinault, while small parties mapped the rivers on either side. A copper box was to go on top of Mount Olympus. Parts of their trail are still in use.

fact_cards.title: Back to the axe
fact_cards.text: Above the bluff O'Neil's men tried a shortcut. Instead of chopping through fallen timber, they led the mules up the riverbed. Two of their best mules were nearly drowned and lost their loads, and the crew went back to the axe. At another crossing the chief packer, M. Price, jumped into the river and cut four tangled mules free of a logjam.
fact_cards.look: You see the river running fast over cobbles. In 1890 an Army mule train tried walking up a riverbed like this, once.
fact_cards.ranger_line: The Army tried walking its mules up this riverbed in 1890. Nearly lost two. Took the trail after that. So should you.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: O'Neil's report, Senate Doc. 59 (1896).

fact_cards.title: Jumbo's Leap
fact_cards.text: Above the falls a box canyon about eighty feet wide stopped O'Neil's mules. The scouts crossed by swinging on a tree, but the pack train needed nearly a week of bridge-building. The men named the canyon Jumbo's Leap, for an old mastiff-hound who, Robert L. Wood wrote, jumped into it rather than be left behind. Jumbo had already won the men over on a hungry scouting trip.

fact_cards.title: Where the serious work began
fact_cards.text: In mid-July 1890 O'Neil's Camp 4 sat in a little basin about a mile below the falls, at the foot of the canyon. The botanist, Louis Henderson, wrote that here the serious work would begin. From here scouting parties fanned out. One group spent a night by a fire on a thirty-degree slope with no blankets, turning to warm one side and then the other, and melted snow for tea.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: O'Neil's report, Senate Doc. 59 (1896); L. F. Henderson, Steel Points, 1907.

fact_cards.title: Visitors at Five Stream
fact_cards.text: Around July 20, 1890, O'Neil's men had company. Judge James Wickersham's party of men and women, sponsored by the Buckley Banner newspaper, came up the North Fork and stopped at the soldiers' camp near Five Stream. One soldier wrote that the camp looked more like a parlor than a jungle. A glove from that party later went to the top of Olympus in O'Neil's copper box.

fact_cards.title: Camp 9
fact_cards.text: On August 16, 1890, O'Neil's party reached Camp 9, about five miles below the head of the North Fork and two below the divide. From here small parties went out to explore while the rest pushed the mule trail on. O'Neil warned that his botanist had found a poisonous plant, stagger weed, where the mules grazed. Whether today's Nine Stream has anything to do with his camp numbers is not known.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: O'Neil's report, Senate Doc. 59 (1896).

fact_cards.title: Yellow jackets and fire
fact_cards.text: In September 1890 yellow jackets swarmed the north slope of the divide between the Skokomish and the Duckabush, stinging the mules. The men set fires to burn out the nests, and the fires spread across the trail. Two mules rolled more than a hundred feet and had to be left behind. Sergeant Marsh drove the pack train straight through the burning hillside to Hoodsport for supplies, and back again.
fact_cards.look: You see the trail climbing to the divide. In 1890 this slope was burning, and the Army drove its mules through anyway.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: O'Neil's report, Senate Doc. 59 (1896).

fact_cards.title: The Higleys
fact_cards.text: In August 1890 Alfred Higley, a Civil War veteran, and his nineteen-year-old son Orte set out from Hoodsport with three friends. They crossed by the Duckabush and met O'Neil's party at Hart Lake. They camped three weeks on Little O'Neil Creek, then came down the East Fork Quinault in early October and settled at Lake Quinault. Alfred became the valley's postmaster.
fact_cards.look: You see Hart Lake, small and cold. In 1890 a father and son walked through here on their way to a new home.

fact_cards.title: Camp 14
fact_cards.text: On September 6, 1890, O'Neil's trail crew brought the last supplies up to Camp 14, at the foot of Mount Anderson on the divide between the Duckabush and the Quinault. They reported that the mules could go no farther. It seemed, O'Neil wrote, that nothing without wings could get down from that divide. The next morning every man went scouting for a route down.
fact_cards.look: You see the ground drop away toward the Quinault. In 1890 an Army camp up here thought only birds could get down.

fact_cards.title: Like flies coming down a wall
fact_cards.text: A way down was found, and the men built a zigzag mule trail about 3,000 feet into the East Fork Quinault: nearly five miles of switchbacks to make three quarters of a mile. To lighten the loads, each man kept one blanket, half a shelter tent and spare socks. Watching the pack train come down from below, O'Neil thought the mules looked like flies coming down a wall.
fact_cards.look: You see switchbacks folding down toward the valley. The first ones here were cut for mules in 1890.
fact_cards.ranger_line: O'Neil's mules came down this wall in 1890 on switchbacks the soldiers cut. Take your time on the way down. He said downhill was the dangerous part.

fact_cards.title: Names for the expedition
fact_cards.text: O'Neil Pass, O'Neil Peak and O'Neil Creek were named later in honor of the 1890 expedition. So were Mounts Bretherton, Church and Henderson, after its naturalist, a woodsman and its botanist, and Mount Steel, after William Gladstone Steel of Portland, founder of the Oregon Alpine Club, which helped pay for the trip. O'Neil handed out names too, following, as he put it, the custom of explorers.
fact_cards.look: You see O'Neil Pass. It was named years later for the lieutenant whose mule trail came down from this divide in 1890.

fact_cards.title: Valley of a Thousand Waterfalls
fact_cards.text: Local people called this the Valley of a Thousand Waterfalls. A Forest Service recreation planner, F. W. Cleator, suggested the name Enchanted Valley to the Olson brothers of Quinault, who built the chalet here. In September 1890 O'Neil's mules had come down into this valley to Camp 15, and from here a small party set out to climb Mount Olympus.
fact_cards.look: You see walls of rock streaked with falling water. People here called it the Valley of a Thousand Waterfalls.

fact_cards.title: The chalet that moved
fact_cards.text: The Olson brothers' company built this log chalet, finished in August 1931. Everything came in thirteen miles by horse, and in 1934 a bathtub was skidded up on a sled. The Depression ruined the business. In the war, aircraft spotters lived here. In September 2014, with the river eating the bank beneath it, the Park Service jacked the chalet up and pushed it back from the edge. A 2020 study proposed removing it.
fact_cards.look: You see a big log chalet in a meadow, a long way from any road. Someone once skidded a bathtub up here on a sled.
fact_cards.ranger_line: Everything in that chalet came up on horses. Including a bathtub, in 1934. The river's been trying to take it ever since.

fact_cards.title: A slight accident
fact_cards.text: On September 13, 1890, the small party bound for Mount Olympus left O'Neil's Camp 15 and walked down the East Fork. That first night they camped by a creek and named it Fire Creek, on account of what the naturalist Bretherton called a slight accident. His account does not say what the accident was. Whether today's Fire Creek is the same stream is not certain.
fact_cards.look: You see a creek running into the East Fork. In 1890 it got its name from a 'slight accident' nobody explained.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: B. J. Bretherton, Steel Points, 1907.

fact_cards.title: The canyon of the East Fork
fact_cards.text: Coming down the East Fork Quinault in September 1890, O'Neil's pack train got past a dangerous canyon. Just beyond it, yellow jackets stung the mules into a stampede, and one leapt from a bluff to a ledge two hundred feet below. She was carrying the coffee and some of O'Neil's papers. He climbed down to her by hanging on to huckleberry bushes. Exactly where this happened is not known.
fact_cards.look: You see the river deep in its gorge. In 1890 a mule carrying all the coffee went over a bluff somewhere along here.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: O'Neil's report, Senate Doc. 59 (1896).

fact_cards.title: Graves Creek Inn
fact_cards.text: In 1930 the Olson brothers of Quinault built an inn here at Graves Creek, at the start of the trail to their chalet in the Enchanted Valley, thirteen miles up. The Depression ended that business. Forty years earlier, in late September 1890, O'Neil had sent his pack train out from this part of the valley to Hoquiam, on a trail the Hoquiam Board of Trade had cut to meet his.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: Evans, NPS Historic Resource Study (1983); O'Neil's report, Senate Doc. 59 (1896).

fact_cards.title: The first sign of people
fact_cards.text: On May 17, 1890, near where the North Fork meets the main Quinault, the Press party found an empty trapper's cabin. It was the first sign of other people they had seen in about eighty days. That night they ate the last of their flour. Soon after, their raft was swept under a driftwood jam. Barnes saved the pack with the journals, the negatives and the map.
fact_cards.look: You see the North Fork running down to meet the main river. Five hungry men found an empty cabin near here in May 1890.

fact_cards.title: From snow into rain
fact_cards.text: Below the divide, in mid-May 1890, the Press party walked out of the snow and into rain and dark rain forest along the North Fork Quinault. Above them stood peaks they named in their usual way: Mount Zindorf, Mount Lawson, Mount Grady. Zindorf is still used, unofficially, and the name Lawson has drifted to another peak. Grady is gone. The party was nearly out of food.

fact_cards.title: Halfway House
fact_cards.text: The shelter here began in the late 1920s as a stopping place built by the Olympic Chalet Company, halfway up the North Fork to its log chalet at Low Divide. The company meant to sell the wilderness to visitors without building a road through it. The Depression ended the plan, and the company was dissolved in 1936. The name stayed.
fact_cards.look: You see a trail shelter called Halfway House. It was halfway to a chalet that is not there anymore.

fact_cards.title: The Kestner place
fact_cards.text: Anton Kestner, an Austrian immigrant, took up this claim in 1891, and his wife, Josepha, came with their sons the next year. Their first house washed away in a flood. Around 1900 they built one of the most solid houses in the valley, with three barns. Until roads came in the 1920s, the lake and river were their highway. It is the oldest surviving settler's homestead in the park's Quinault valley.
fact_cards.look: You see an old farmhouse and a barn going gray in the rain. An Austrian family homesteaded here in 1891.

fact_cards.title: Antrim's canoe
fact_cards.text: On May 18 or 19, 1890, the starving Press party was found by Frederick Antrim, a settler from Aberdeen, travelling by canoe with two Quinault men. Antrim took them to his cabin near Lake Quinault and fed them. The party later named an Antrim Range for him. They reached the lake on May 19, and on May 20 they came down the river by canoe to the Pacific.

fact_cards.title: Lake Quinault
fact_cards.text: The lake and the river carry the name of the Quinault people. The lake's waters have been part of the Quinault Indian Reservation since before 1900, and the Quinault Indian Nation sets the rules on it. Quinault canoes carried many early travelers: the Gilmans up the river in 1889, the Press party down it in 1890, and The Mountaineers thirty-five miles to the sea in 1920.

fact_cards.title: The Gilmans
fact_cards.text: In October 1889 Charles Gilman, once lieutenant governor of Minnesota, and his son Samuel, an engineer, were taken about thirty miles up the Quinault by canoe by a Quinault man travelling with his wife and baby. They climbed several peaks and saw little but fog until one clear day in November. Samuel wrote about the country for National Geographic in 1896. He died at thirty-six, before he knew it was accepted.

fact_cards.title: Mount Seattle
fact_cards.text: On April 29, 1890, the Press party's leader, James Christie, and its photographer, Charles Barnes, named the big peak above this creek Mount Seattle, for the city that had sent them. Nearby Mount Noyes was named for Crosby Noyes of the Washington Evening Star. Both names are still on the map, and so is this creek.

fact_cards.title: The 1920 outing
fact_cards.text: In August 1920 about eighty Mountaineers walked from Brinnon over Hayden Pass, down the Hayes to the Elwha, across to the Quinault, and up a brand-new trail along the high divide between the Quinault and the Queets. When their head packer fell ill and a helper quit, they voted to go on and lead the horses themselves. They finished with a thirty-five-mile canoe trip down the Quinault to the sea.
fact_cards.look: You see a high ridge trail between two great valleys. In 1920 it was brand new, and eighty climbers walked it.
fact_cards.credit_line: Sources: The Mountaineer, 1920.

fact_cards.title: Shoe leather
fact_cards.text: In August 1890 two of O'Neil's people, the settler Frederic Church and a newly arrived doctor, set off to explore the Satsop, the Wynoochee and the Wishkah. Church fell on a bluff, broke his compass and lost food. For five days the two lived on berries, and the doctor had his first taste of shoe leather. A government geographer later wrote that the Wynoochee was named for its shifting course.

fact_cards.title: Black Creek
fact_cards.text: The Wilkes Expedition of the U.S. Navy charted this river as Black Creek in 1841. The name did not last. Skokomish is a Twana word; a missionary of the 1890s gave it the meaning river people, but that is his reading. It is also the name of the Skokomish Indian Tribe, whose homeland includes this valley.

fact_cards.title: The timber cruisers
fact_cards.text: From 1898 to 1900 two timber cruisers, Arthur Dodwell and Theodore Rixon, walked the new Olympic Forest Reserve township by township for the U.S. Geological Survey and made the first map of the whole range. They counted about 61 billion board feet of timber. Their report warned that off the trails the brush was nearly impossible to push through, that old trails were growing over, and that a river in flood was a dangerous place to be.

fact_cards.title: Semple Plateau
fact_cards.text: In early April 1890 the Press party worked up the Elwha past a great landslide toward a flat bench above the west bank. They named it Semple Plateau, for Eugene Semple, a former governor of Washington Territory. There was no water on top, but springs ran out all around, just below its rim. Barnes believed it had been the site of a village long before. The snow at their camps was waist deep.

fact_cards.title: Lakes Francis and John
fact_cards.text: In 1890 Lt. O'Neil gave the names Francis and John to two lakes at the head of the Duckabush. His report does not say which two. expeditions.name: Sailors' names on the coast
expeditions.summary_own_words: Spanish and British ships charted the coast and named what they could see from the water: Santa Rosalia and then Mount Olympus, Isla de Dolores and Destruction Island, the Port of Our Lady of the Angels, Cape Alava, Cape Flattery and Flattery Rocks, New Dungeness. They told their side only; the coast's peoples were already there.

expeditions.name: The Gilmans
expeditions.summary_own_words: Father and son went up the Quinault by Quinault canoe in October 1889, walked the west side from the Sol Duc to the Quinault mouth that winter, and reported soberly on land, timber and minerals. Samuel's article appeared in National Geographic in 1896.

expeditions.name: Banta and Sharp
expeditions.summary_own_words: Two Tacoma men scouted the Queets for homestead land with Native canoe help, then sold a colony plan; thirty-one claims by spring 1890.

expeditions.name: The Seattle Press Exploring Expedition
expeditions.summary_own_words: Six men (five finished), four dogs and two mules crossed the range north to south in winter and spring: up the Elwha from Port Angeles, over Low Divide on May 5, and down the North Fork Quinault to Lake Quinault and the sea. The first documented crossing of the range. Their report filled the Seattle Press of July 16, 1890.

After Robert L. Wood, 'The O'Neil Expeditions', Columbia (1990), p. 42 sidebar

expeditions.name: The Olympic Exploring Expedition (O'Neil and the Oregon Alpine Club)
expeditions.summary_own_words: Soldiers and Oregon Alpine Club scientists cut a mule trail of about 93 miles from Hood Canal up the North Fork Skokomish, over First Divide and O'Neil Pass and down the East Fork Quinault, while foot parties mapped the southern half of the range. A side party left a copper box on a summit of Olympus. O'Neil's report proposed a national park.

After Robert L. Wood, 'The O'Neil Expeditions', Columbia (1990), pp. 41-45

expeditions.name: Wickersham's Buckley Banner party
expeditions.summary_own_words: Men and women went up the North Fork Skokomish, met O'Neil's soldiers near Five Stream, turned east by mistake and came out down the Dosewallips, about 125 miles in all. Wickersham then drew the first known map outlining a park.

expeditions.name: The Higleys
expeditions.summary_own_words: A father and son crossed from Hoodsport by the Duckabush, met O'Neil's party at Hart Lake, and came down the East Fork Quinault to settle at Lake Quinault.

expeditions.name: The Dodwell-Rixon survey
expeditions.summary_own_words: USGS timber cruisers walked the Olympic Forest Reserve township by township for three seasons and made the first topographic map of the whole range. Their packer made the first recorded climb of Olympus's East Peak.

expeditions.name: The Mountaineers' first outing
expeditions.summary_own_words: Sixty-five people walked up the Elwha to a main camp in Elwha Basin, climbed many peaks, were turned back once by a gale, and made the first ascent of Olympus's West Peak on Aug. 13, 1907.

wood.credit: After Robert L. Wood, The Land That Slept Late (1995), ch. 'The Olympic Summer Outings', p. 131

expeditions.name: Three summits in a day
expeditions.summary_own_words: Four Bremerton men (George Hannaman, H. H. Botten, William Spaulding and Alex Ormond) climbed one of the Five Fingers in cloud by mistake, then the West, Middle and East peaks of Olympus the same day.
