expeditions.name: The 1920 outing
expeditions.summary_own_words: About eighty Mountaineers walked from Brinnon up the Dosewallips, over Hayden Pass to the Elwha, climbed Olympus's Middle Peak and Mount Anderson's east peak, crossed Low Divide, followed the new trail along the Quinault-Queets divide and canoed down the Quinault to Taholah.

expeditions.name: Bob Wood's Bailey Range climbs
expeditions.summary_own_words: Reported first ascents of Mount Childs, Mount Pulitzer and Stephen Peak; the 'Bob Wood' is very probably the historian.

events.event: Juan Perez sees the great snowy mountain and names it Santa Rosalia.
Spanish sailors are killed ashore near the Hoh; Bodega y Quadra names the island Isla de Dolores.
Barkley names the Hoh 'Destruction River' after men from his ship are killed on shore; the name later moves to the island.
John Meares names Mount Olympus.
Manuel Quimper's chart names Cape Alava.
Francisco de Eliza names the harbor the Port of Our Lady of the Angels; his chart calls the Lyre the Rio Cuesta.
Vancouver charts Mount Olympus, names New Dungeness and Flattery Rocks; the Spanish briefly fortify Neah Bay.
The Wilkes Expedition charts the Skokomish as Black Creek.
Kellett's chart puts the names Elwha, River Lyre and Neah Bay on the map.
The Makah sign the Treaty of Neah Bay, keeping whaling, sealing and fishing rights.
The Treaty of Quinault River (signed again at Olympia in 1856), to which the Quinault, Quileute and Hoh trace their treaty rights.
George Davidson names Mount Constance, Mount Ellinor and The Brothers from Puget Sound.
S'Klallam families under Lord James Balch buy 210 acres at Jamestown for $500 in gold.
Lts. Wittich and Bradley cut a trail across both forks of the Dungeness.
O'Neil, a young 14th Infantry lieutenant at Fort Townsend, stares at the Olympics across the water and finds that nobody can tell him anything reliable about the interior.

Cutting trail toward a peak O'Neil called Mount Sherman (now Mount Angeles), the party crosses the first ridge by a pass near the peak ('Victors Pass') to the head of a stream they call Hawgood Creek. O'Neil's compass needle swings near a body of magnetic iron.
From the heights O'Neil called The Sisters (Mount Angeles and Klahhane Ridge) he looks south over a wild jumble of peaks and takes one cluster for Mount Olympus.
After a transfer to Vancouver Barracks, O'Neil talks Gen. Nelson A. Miles into an exploration; the order is signed by Asst. Adj. Gen. H. Clay Wood.

The party leaves Port Angeles (then about forty people, a hotel, a sawmill and two stores) heading south into the foothills: up the Ennis Creek country (Evans), on a line much like today's Hurricane Ridge Road (NPS). Their Native guide leaves them the first night. It takes about a month to reach Hurricane Ridge.
At the foot of the first snowy range. Long days on thin rations; mules keep tumbling off the steep sidehills.

On Hurricane Ridge the party splits. Engineer Harry Hawgood's group heads down toward the Elwha but loses its supplies in a river crossing and turns back; O'Neil's group follows the high divide south and east. Elk and deer are everywhere and the open ridges have little brush.

The mules stop at a camp O'Neil names Noplace, probably in Cameron Basin. O'Neil and Pvt. John Johnson go on foot toward the Mount Anderson country, get separated, and Johnson walks out alone. O'Neil locates and names Mount Claywood (for H. Clay Wood).
A courier brings orders sending O'Neil to Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. He sails from Port Angeles with the work unfinished. He later writes that the hardships were worth it.

Back in the Northwest from 1887, O'Neil becomes secretary of the new Oregon Alpine Club (Portland, founded 1887 by William G. Steel and others). The club and the Army agree on a joint expedition: the club pays most costs and sends three scientists; Gen. John Gibbon supplies O'Neil, soldiers, a packer, mules and dogs.
A one-square-mile Quileute reservation is set aside at La Push; later that year a settler burns all 26 houses in the village.
The Seattle Press prints an interview with Gov. Elisha P. Ferry calling the interior an unknown land and daring 'hardy citizens' to explore it.
The Gilmans go up the Quinault by Quinault canoe.
The Press receives James Christie's letter from North Yakima offering to lead a party into the Olympics that winter.
The six men are photographed in Seattle before leaving.
The party leaves Seattle by steamer (the Evangel) for Port Angeles. A Sacramento paper later said Dec 7; the Port Angeles Commonwealth said they arrived on a Monday (Dec 9).
Banta and Sharp head south from the Sol Duc toward the Queets.
They leave the end of the county road out of Port Angeles for the Elwha (Seattle Times date). Snow fell on their first night in camp and stopped at about four feet (SDRU1890).
Christmas snow; supplies are moved by sled toward the river.
The boat Gertie is launched loaded with supplies and leaks at once; the men spend days caulking her.
A Port Townsend paper reports the party back at Port Angeles 'last evening' with two feet of snow within ten miles of town (probably a supply trip; the report credits Barnes as the man in charge).
Gertie is finally watertight and the haul up the Elwha begins.
Barnes's journal: barely a quarter mile gained, two sets of rapids, a log cut out, everyone in the icy river to the belt at 16 degrees F, Crumback close to fainting.
A log jam at the mouth of Indian Creek stops the boat; local men help drag her over.
Head of navigation: stores are moved ashore and Gertie is abandoned, after 10-12 days and only a few miles. From here the men relay packs and use the mules.
Snowbound for about two weeks in an empty settler's cabin, then relaying about forty 50-lb packs by snowshoe and sled. Moving 800 lb a mile and a half could take a whole day.
On the Devil's Backbone, a steep ridge above today's old Elwha Ranger Station, the mule Jennie falls to her death with the fireworks.
They spend a night in an abandoned Klallam house near the site of the later Glines Canyon dam, and meet a Klallam elk-hunting camp near today's park boundary.
Dr. Runnalls leaves the expedition. Five men go on.
The party reaches the area of Griff Creek on the Elwha.
South end of what later became Lake Mills: beyond here nobody in the settlements could tell them anything. Half the supplies are already gone.
A member kills a bobcat where a creek meets the Elwha; they call it Wildcat Creek (today's Cat Creek).
Goblin Gates: the whole Elwha pours through a slot of rock about 12 ft wide. Barnes sees faces in the rock and names it. Christie catches fourteen trout in half an hour nearby; deer show no fear.
Geyser Valley: they hear booming bursts that speed up and stop, every few days, and decide they must be geysers. They build a smokehouse and live on elk, deer and steelhead. Everyone has dysentery.
Barnes finds very old blazes healed into tree trunks (one with about 210 growth rings over the cut) and old 'wringing posts' used to dress hides, between Geyser Valley and the Lillian River.
Crumback stakes a squatter's claim by the river.

Up the Elwha past a great landslide and the 'Semple Plateau', a flat bench on the west side that Barnes takes for an old village site, into the wide upper valley they call Press Valley. Waist-deep snow at camp. In April, gunshots near the main camp set off a scare about strangers.
The dog Dike is killed by a bull elk in Press Valley.

Climbing out of the Goldie with 75-lb packs through snow said to be up to 15 ft deep. From the high ground Christie and Barnes see over the divide ahead, and from then on it is 'one pack to a man', no more relaying.
They reach the Lillian River, which they name.
A scouting party sees a gap leading away from the Elwha. The party turns up the Goldie River: the wrong way, into steep, trackless side country. Around now the exhausted mule Dollie is turned loose.
They name the Bailey Range, after the Press's owner William E. Bailey.
Christie and Barnes name Mount Seattle for the city.
Just past the divide, with almost nothing left but flour soup, the dogs bring three bears to bay. The meat (and the men drinking bear grease straight from the pan) saves them from starving.
Snow gives way to rain and dark rain forest on the North Fork Quinault. They pass the Rustler Creek confluence in mid-May.
Camp in the upper Goldie drainage below Mount Wilder; then they drop back to the upper Elwha valley floor (about four hours down).
Up the last of the Elwha, past the place later called Chicago Camp, toward the gap between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie.

They name Lake Mary and Lake Margaret and find the pass, which they call Elwha Pass (today's Low Divide, 3,602 ft in our data). A hole in the snow by a big rock shows water running south: they are over the top.
At the junction of the North Fork and the main Quinault they find an empty trapper's cabin, the first sign of other people in about 80 days. That night they eat the last of the flour.
Their raft is swept under a driftwood jam. They lose guns, ammunition, bear skins, fishing tackle and most rock samples. Barnes saves the pack with the journals, about 250 negatives and the map.
Settler Frederick S. Antrim of Aberdeen and two Quinault men in a canoe find them; Antrim later canoes them to his cabin near Lake Quinault and feeds them.
They reach Lake Quinault.
By canoe down the lake and river to the Quinault Indian Agency at the river mouth (Taholah), on the Pacific.
Five ragged men sail into Aberdeen at 2 a.m.; telegrams from the Press are waiting. Photographed in their rags.
Back in Seattle, 166 days after leaving.
O'Neil leaves Vancouver Barracks for Puget Sound to prepare. He has the Seattle Press party's report (published July 16) in mind and thinks a winter crossing was a mistake.

The pack train leaves Vancouver Barracks under Sgt. Marsh with packer Price and Pvt. Barnes; the rest follow on the 25th and reach Fort Townsend on the 27th. The hired steamer Enterprise has burst her boilers, so the steamer Louise of Port Hadlock is chartered.
The Evening Star reports Christie hired as foreman of the National Geographic Society's Mount St. Elias expedition, taking two famous bear dogs.

A box canyon only about 80 feet wide and deep stops the mules near Camp 5. Scouts cross by swinging on a tree; the pack train needs nearly a week of bridge-building. The men name it Jumbo's Leap. A mule rolls down the canyon side and is badly hurt.

Judge James Wickersham's family party (sponsored by the Buckley Banner) passes the camp, bound for Port Angeles; they end up descending the Dosewallips to Hood Canal after hard going. O'Neil later hears that one of them was badly poisoned.

Overnight run down Hood Canal. No dock at the mouth of Lilliwaup Creek: supplies go ashore in small boats and the mules are pushed off the deck to swim. The trail to Lake Cushman, sold to them as good and six miles long, is steep, wet and choked with windfall. Henderson walks ahead alone, botanizing, and needs ten and a half hours. The main party camps in a swamp at 9 p.m. after about 2.5 miles; one mule wedges under a log and has to be cut out.

Lake Cushman reached at noon. Everything is ferried over on settler Rose's old raft, and camp is made in Mr. Windoffer's field on the west shore. The night before, the advance party at the lake had almost nothing to eat until foragers brought bacon and bread and O'Neil walked in with a full haversack; the first mules straggled in at 6 p.m. on the 3rd.
Independence Day off duty. The men fish; Henderson lands about a hundred trout in a few hours.
Scouts look for a way up the Skokomish while O'Neil finds a better supply trail from Hoodsport. Settler Frederic Church joins as a volunteer woodsman. It rains without letup.

Trail cut about 4.5 miles to Camp 2, near a camp of copper miners (the end of any existing trail). A bluff at the river's edge blocks the way, so the men fell trees against its face and cover them with dirt and boughs to make a mule ledge; it takes four and a half days. Krause, crippled by rheumatism, is relieved on July 8.
Trail reaches Camp 3, about 7 miles above the lake. Trying to travel up the riverbed instead of chopping through windfall nearly drowns two mules and loses their loads; the crew goes back to the axe.

Henderson and Pvt. Fisher climb a high peak west of Lake Cushman (probably Mount Lincoln) and see Hood Canal, Mount Rainier and, far to the northwest, Olympus. They stumble back into camp at 9:30 p.m.
Camp 4 is set in a little basin about a mile below the falls, at the foot of the Canyon. Henderson calls it the point where the serious work begins.

Scouting parties fan out. Henderson, Linsley and Sgt. Yates go up the South Branch, followed against their wishes by the hound Jumbo, who wins them over. They sleep by a fire on a 30-degree slope with no blankets and melt snow for tea. Another party reaches 'Bruins Peak' and first sees the East Fork Quinault; two visiting hunters who came along never ask to join again.
The Seattle Press publishes the report (Wednesday evening): a 24-page edition, with the story on 10 to 16 pages, many engravings from Barnes's photographs, and his map.

Church and Bretherton set out to map the South Fork Skokomish on short rations (three days' worth per O'Neil; Henderson says five on one page and three on the next). It takes them well over a week, the last days nearly foodless; hunters from Olympia help them out.
Dr. J. Church (a physician just out from Washington, D.C.) joins the party.

Camp 6 above the falls (July 27) and Camp 7 by a big snowbank at only 2,300 feet (July 28). Henderson slashes his wrist cutting fir boughs for bedding. Scouts report the line is impossible for mules; everyone falls back to Camp 6 by July 30.

After nine days out, Sgts. Marsh and Yates and Pvt. Fisher return: a route goes up the North Fork to its head, over a divide into an unknown valley (it proves to be the Duckabush). They kill several elk; until then the only fresh meat had been a deer or a bear shot by earlier scouts. All hands move to the new line.
Five hard days down the Quinault to the lake, a few hours as guests of a settler, then three days to Humptulips City ('two houses and a name') and twelve days on the Humptulips and Hoquiam rivers.

Three scouting parties leave Camp 6 in a downpour with orders not to return until their routes prove impossible or safe. On Aug. 3 Henderson heads home with Pvt. Higgins and the mule Frenchy, leaving his plant press with Pvt. Fisher.

Camp 9 is reached, about 5 miles below the head of the North Fork and 2 miles below the divide. From here small parties are sent out while the rest push the mule trail on. O'Neil warns of poisonous 'stagger weed' where the mules graze.

Foot parties depart. Church and Dr. Church head for the Satsop, Wynoochee and Wishkah; Bretherton and Sgt. Yates for the Duckabush and Dosewallips; O'Neil with Pvts. Fisher and Danton for the East Fork Quinault, Lake Quinault and the Humptulips.

O'Neil's party leaves at 5:30 a.m. with 50 lb each, hauls up 2,500 feet by huckleberry bushes, inches along a slate ledge for an hour and a half, and at 5 p.m. tops the Quinault divide to see the snowy main range. Going down, a broad elk trail ends at a cliff; they spend the night in a gully. Next morning Danton nearly falls from a ledge. By noon they reach the East Fork Quinault, which heads under Mount Anderson's glaciers.

The side parties suffer: Church falls on a Satsop bluff, ruins his compass and loses food, and he and the doctor live on berries for five days (the doctor tries shoe leather); Bretherton and Yates trace the Duckabush and Dosewallips to Hood Canal.

At Hoquiam the Board of Trade offers to cut a trail from town to meet the expedition's if O'Neil will use it (done by Sept. 25). He goes back by steamer and rail to Union City and walks his own trail to camp in three days.

A route is found, and a zigzag mule trail is built down about 3,000 feet into the East Fork Quinault, nearly five miles of trail to make three-quarters of a mile. Camp 15 is made on the Quinault side. Extra gear goes back: each man keeps one blanket, half a shelter tent, spare socks and underwear. A month of food is kept.

Yellow-jackets infest the north slope of the Skokomish-Duckabush divide. Fires set to burn the nests spread over the trail. Two mules roll more than 100 feet and are left; Sgt. Marsh forces the pack train through the burning hillside to Hoodsport for stores and back. (One of the abandoned mules, B. C., later died near Lake Cushman; the other died at Hoodsport.)

Fisher gives up trying to rejoin and follows the Queets to the ocean. Short of boots and food, Linsley also takes the Queets instead of the assigned Hoh and Quillayute (thinking at first it was the Hoh), passes the Quinault agency on Sept. 29 and goes on to Hoquiam. O'Neil is not pleased.

The pack train descends from the divide into the East Fork Quinault ('like flies coming down a wall') and makes the forks in about five days. Just past the dangerous canyon, yellow-jackets stampede the mules; one leaps the bluff and dies on a ledge 200 feet down with the coffee and O'Neil's papers. The mule Sorais also rolled into the Quinault gorge (the report does not say when).

Linsley and Sgt. Marsh with eight men finish the trail to the foot of Mount Anderson and bring up all supplies. At Camp 14, on the Duckabush-Quinault divide, they report that the mules can go no farther.
All parties are back in camp, and every man is sent scouting for a route down.

The Linsley party (Linsley, Bretherton, Sgt. Yates, Pvts. Fisher, Danton, Kranichfeld, Hughes) leaves with 25 days' food: find the Elwha's source, place the Oregon Alpine Club's copper box on Olympus, then explore the Hoh and Quillayute. First night: a creek they name Fire Creek 'on account of a slight accident'; next day yellow-jackets on the climb to the divide.

They cross into the Elwha headwaters, camp on a park-like saddle they name Bretherton's Pass, lose a day to fog, cross a 5,500-foot ridge (Sept. 17) and reach the Elwha above its forks, where they find a joke poem left at an old camp.

Up a long glacier to the head of the Queets; across 'Pluto's Gulch' to a flowery plateau they call the Garden of the Gods. Pvt. Fisher is separated in an alder thicket; that night they see his fire far below from a camp on the edge of a 5,200-foot drop.

Linsley, Bretherton and Danton climb to a summit of Mount Olympus from the south and leave the copper box (with a record book and trinkets: a pencil, a glove from the Wickersham party, cards, army buttons, a beer check, shoelaces, a visiting card, three cablegrams). Wood judged it probably a crag of the South Peak, not the true top. The box has never been found. O'Neil believed no one had stood there before (i.e., first recorded by settlers).

The pack train is sent out to Hoquiam on the Board of Trade trail. O'Neil, Frederic Church, Dr. Church and a Mr. West head for the head of the North Fork Quinault, finding many old Seattle Press camps; Sgt. Marsh and McCarty cross toward the Humptulips.

Canyon Creek gorge in the rain; a view of the Queets and of Olympus 'with its forty glaciers'. Church and the doctor go down the Queets; O'Neil and West look for the Raft River, take a bad tumble (one broken finger, the worst injury of the expedition), lose O'Neil's watch and food in a pool, and follow a stream that vanishes underground for three hours. O'Neil names it the West Branch.

At Lake Quinault after three days of rain, then two days by canoe down the Quinault River in the rain. A Quinault family takes O'Neil in for a night and feeds him; on Sept. 30 he reaches the Quinault agency at the river mouth.
The rival Post-Intelligencer reprints a later party's complaint that the Press blazes give out and that no geysers could be heard.
O'Neil reaches Hoquiam on Oct. 1. The explorers are feted there (Oct. 4), disband (Oct. 6) and are given a banquet by the Oregon Alpine Club in Portland (Oct. 22).

O'Neil submits his report at Vancouver Barracks: the outer slopes are valuable, the interior is useless for settlement but would make a fine national park, chiefly to save the elk. He repeats the idea in a Portland lecture on Dec. 6.
Anton Kestner takes up his Quinault claim; John Huelsdonk settles on the upper Hoh about now.
Three men bound for the Pacific leave a note in a baking-powder can on the Elwha-Queets pass.
Admiral Beardslee's catch at Lake Crescent gives the Beardslee trout its name.

At the request of UW president Mark W. Harrington, the report is printed as Senate Doc. 59 and referred to the Select Committee on Forest Reservations and the Protection of Game. The map, photographs and scientists' reports were not included.
S. C. Gilman's 'The Olympic Country' appears in National Geographic.
Will Humes and his relatives arrive on the upper Elwha; Grant follows in 1899.
President Cleveland creates the Olympic Forest Reserve.
Jack McGlone of the USGS survey climbs Olympus's East Peak and leaves a Shelton newspaper.
Dodwell and Rixon's survey is published as USGS Professional Paper 7.
The Norwegian bark Prince Arthur is wrecked south of Cape Alava; 18 of 20 die.
The Spruce post office opens in the Huelsdonk home on the Hoh; the Hoh post office opens near the river mouth.
Storm King Ranger Station is built (about this year).
Marymere, the first resort hotel on Barnes Point, opens.
The great Sol Duc fire; Chris Morgenroth later leads the replanting of a 13,000-acre burn.
Seventeen years on, The Mountaineers say they know nothing of what O'Neil's 1890 party accomplished; that summer Steel Points prints Bretherton's and Henderson's accounts.
A New York party guided by Will Humes climbs Olympus's Middle Peak and names Dodwell-Rixon Pass and Humes Glacier.
The Mountaineers' first Olympus attempt is turned back by a gale; Winona Bailey falls and survives.
Eleven Mountaineers make the first ascent of Olympus's West Peak.
Four Bremerton men climb all three Olympus summits in one day.
Olympic Hot Springs opens to the public.
Theodore Roosevelt proclaims Mount Olympus National Monument (Proclamation 869).
Mount Olympus National Monument (1909) and Olympic National Park (June 29, 1938) follow. O'Neil, by then a general, dies about a month after the park is created.
Work begins on the Elwha Dam (running by 1913).
Michael Earles's hotel opens at Sol Duc Hot Springs.
Campers name Mount Gladys.
Fire destroys the Sol Duc hotel.
The last rail of the Spruce Railroad is laid, after the armistice.
The Mountaineers' 1920 outing leaves Brinnon.
Thirteen Mountaineers climb Mount Anderson's east peak.
The schooner-barge W. J. Pirrie breaks up near Cape Johnson in a gale.
The Cushman dam raises Lake Cushman and drowns the old resorts.
Glines Canyon Dam is finished; the Low Divide chalet opens.
Mount Olympus National Monument is closed to hunting and trapping.
The Enchanted Valley chalet is finished.
The CCC opens Camp Elwha; the Forest Service builds the Dodger Point lookout; the monument passes to the Park Service.
Franklin Roosevelt visits Port Angeles and spends the night at Lake Crescent.
Congress creates Olympic National Park; Preston Macy becomes its first superintendent.
The Army builds an Aircraft Warning Service lookout on Pyramid Peak.
An avalanche destroys the Low Divide chalet.
Robert L. Wood first sees the Olympics.
Wood writes a University of Washington term paper on the Olympic rain forest, the seed of his books.
Bob Wood, Doug Waali and Kent Heathershaw make reported first ascents in the Bailey Range.
The Park Service buys Sol Duc Hot Springs and closes the Olympic Hot Springs resort.
Wood's Across the Olympic Mountains: The Press Expedition, 1889-90 is published.
Wood's Trail Country: Olympic National Park is published.
Wood's Men, Mules, and Mountains: Lieutenant O'Neil's Olympic Expeditions is published.
The Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe wins federal recognition.
Wood's Olympic Mountains Trail Guide is published (new editions 1991, 2000, 2020).
Congress passes the Elwha River Ecosystem and Fisheries Restoration Act.
Wood's The Land That Slept Late is published.
Robert L. Wood dies, aged 78.
Removal of the Elwha dams begins; both are gone by 2014.
The Enchanted Valley chalet is moved back from the eroding riverbank.

place_names.name: Mount Olympus (and the Olympic Mountains)
place_names.origin_own_words: The Spanish captain Juan Perez saw the mountain in 1774 and called it Santa Rosalia. On 4 July 1788 the British trader John Meares named it Mount Olympus; Vancouver kept the name on his 1792 chart, and over the next century the whole range came to be called the Olympic Mountains.
place_names.notes: Meany's elevation figure (8,150 ft) is the 1923 value; modern surveys put the West Peak lower (see elevation_ft for mount_olympus_west_peak in hoh_olympus.json). 'Discovered' is Meany's 1923 word; the peninsula's peoples knew the mountain long before.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Mount Olympus, highest peak in the Olympic Mountains, in the north central portion of Jefferson County. Elevation, 8,150 feet. (United States Geological Survey: A Dictionary of Altitudes, page 1022.) The mountain was discovered by the Spanish Captain, Juan Perez, in 1774 and named by him “El Cero de la Santa Rosalia.” (Pacific Railroad Reports, Volume XII., Part I., page 262.) The Spanish chart was not published until years had elapsed. On July 4, 1788, the British Captain, John Meares, saw the mountain and named it Mount Olympus. Captain George Vancouver saw the mountain in 1792 and charted the name as given by Captain Meares. (Voyage of Discovery, second edition, Volume II., pages 41-42.) The name has remained on all subsequent maps.
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meany (p. 199) passes on two outsiders' reports of Native names for the mountains. A modern writer has questioned one of them. Do not print any Native name for Olympus unless the tribes confirm it.

place_names.name: Hurricane Hill (and Hurricane Ridge)
place_names.origin_own_words: Probably named for its fierce winds, according to an Elwha settler who wrote to Meany.
place_names.notes: Meany has no separate entry for Hurricane Ridge. H. B. Herrick was an Elwha valley packer; his 1900 note was found in a can on the Elwha-Queets pass in 1907 (see topic prospectors_1890s).

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Hurricane Hill, near Elwha, in Clallam County. Probably named on account of the velocity of winds there at times. (H. B. Herrick, Elwha, in Names MSS., Letter 267.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Elwha River
place_names.origin_own_words: The name was first charted by the British (Kellett, 1847). Meany reports, from the missionary Myron Eells (1892), that the Native word means 'elk'.
place_names.notes: 'Anthropolgist' is the 1923 misprint. McDonald (Elwha) was where the 1907 Mountaineers left the stage road and 'hit the trail'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Elwha River, rising in the Olympic Mountains, it flows into the Strait of Juan de Fuca near Port Angeles, in the northern part of Clallam County. The name first appears on the British Admiralty Chart 1911, Kellett, 1847, and on all subsequent maps, though the spelling has not always been the same. Rev. Myron Eells says the Indian word means “Elk.” (American Anthropolgist, January, 1892.) On the bank of the river, seven miles west of Port Angeles, there is a town formerly known as “McDonald,” but now called Elwha. (H. B. Herrick, in Names MSS., Letter 267.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: The meaning 'elk' comes from a non-Native missionary. Ask the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe before presenting any meaning as fact.

place_names.name: Port Angeles (also Mount Angeles, Lake Angeles)
place_names.origin_own_words: Spanish: in 1791 Francisco de Eliza named the harbor 'Port of Our Lady of the Angels'; it was shortened by Galiano and Valdes (1792) and by Vancouver to the present form. Mount Angeles and Lake Angeles take their names from the town (our inference; Meany has no entries for them).

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Port Angeles, county seat of Clallam County. The name originated with the Spaniards in 1791, Captain Francisco Eliza named the peculiar harbor “Porto de Nuestra Senora de los Angeles;” in 1792, Captains Galliano and Valdes contracted it to “Porto de los Angeles.” Captain Vancouver shortened it still further in 1792 and gave the form now in use. In 1852, the United States Coast Survey charted it as “False Dungeness” from its resemblance to New Dungeness nearby. The long sandspit which makes the harbor is called Ediz Hook, probably from Yennis, Clallam Indian word, meaning “good place.” See Ediz Hook.
meany_1923_verbatim.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); remainder from archive.org OCR
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: The Klallam word and its meaning are Meany's report; confirm with the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe before use.

place_names.name: Lake Crescent
place_names.origin_own_words: Before 1890 it was Lake Everett or Big Lake. Boosters of the townsite of Port Crescent, seven miles away, and the editor of the Port Crescent Leader pushed the name Lake Crescent, which stuck.
place_names.notes: Crescent Bay on the Strait (Kellett, 1847) is named for its shape (Meany p. 61).

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Lake Crescent, in the northern part of Clallam County. Up to 1890, the lake was variously known as Lake Everett, Big Lake and Lake Crescent. In that year the Port Crescent Improvement Company was booming its townsite, which was but seven miles from the lake. M. J. Carrigan started the Port Crescent Leader and agitated the beauties and name of the lake. The name is now well established. The lake has become a great resort, reached mostly by way of Port Angeles. (D. A. Christopher, Piedmont, in Names MSS., Letter 252.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Fairholm(e)
place_names.origin_own_words: Mrs. George E. Machelle suggested the name when the post office opened in 1893; in 1913 she asked that town and post office be renamed Lake Crescent. The trailhead uses the later spelling 'Fairholme'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Fairholm, a town on Lake Crescent in Clallam County, which had that name for about ten years. It was suggested by Mrs. George E. Machelle when the postoffice was established in 1893. She requested in 1913 that the name of the town and postoffice be changed to Lake Crescent, which was done. (D. A. Christopher, Piedmont, in Names MSS., Letter 252.)
meany_1923_verbatim.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); remainder from archive.org OCR
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Piedmont (north shore of Lake Crescent)
place_names.origin_own_words: Named in 1893 by William Dawson for its place at the foot of a mountain (Italian/French 'foot of the mountain'). The 1914-15 county ferries Majority and Storm King were launched here (HRS ch. 4).

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Piedmont, a town on the shore of Lake Crescent, in the north central part of Clallam County. It was named in 1893 by William Dawson on account of its position at the foot of a mountain. (D. A. Christopher, in Names MSS. Letter 252.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Lyre River
place_names.origin_own_words: Eliza's Spanish chart of 1791 called it Rio Cuesta; the British surveyor Kellett renamed it River Lyre in 1847.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Lyre River, flowing into the Strait of Juan de Fuca in the northern part of Clallam County. Captain Eliza's Spanish chart of 1791 shows it as “Rio Cuesta.” (United States Public Documents, Serial Number 1557, chart K.) Captain Kellett changed it in 1847 to River Lyre on the British Admiralty chart 1911. It appears as Lyre River on all present day charts.
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Barnes Point and Barnes Creek (Lake Crescent)
place_names.origin_own_words: Sarah Barnes and her son Paul staked a claim near the mouth of the creek about 1890; the Barnes family's point and creek kept their name. Not the same Barnes as Capt. Charles A. Barnes of the Press Expedition (Mount Barnes).
place_names.notes: The game calls the lodge on Barnes Point 'Stillwater Lodge'. Historically: Marymere resort (1906, burned about 1914), Rosemary Inn (1914; named for Rose Littleton and her assistant Mary Daum) and Singer's Tavern (1915, later Lake Crescent Lodge).

place_names.name: Marymere Falls
place_names.origin_own_words: The falls share their name with Marymere, the first resort hotel on Barnes Point (1906), run by Rose Littleton with her assistant Mary Daum. Who first applied the name to the falls is not confirmed in our sources.
place_names.confidence: low for the falls' naming; high for the 1906 resort

place_names.name: Mount Storm King and Storm King Ranger Station
place_names.origin_own_words: The ranger station (about 1905) is one of the oldest Forest Service buildings on the peninsula and is tied to ranger Chris Morgenroth. In 1915 a county ferry on the lake was christened Storm King. We have not found a documented origin for the mountain's name.
place_names.indigenous_caution: Lake Crescent and Mount Storm King figure in Klallam and Quileute oral tradition. Do not retell or adapt any such story; consult the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe and the Quileute Tribe.

place_names.name: Morgenroth Lake (Seven Lakes Basin)
place_names.origin_own_words: Very probably named for Chris Morgenroth (German-born Bogachiel homesteader, Forest Service ranger from 1903-05, builder of trails in the upper Bogachiel and Hoh, leader of the replanting of the 1907 Sol Duc burn, and a witness for the national park in the 1930s). We have not yet found the naming record itself.
place_names.confidence: medium (namesake probable, naming record not seen)
place_names.notes: This is the game creator's favorite spot; Morgenroth's reforestation story suits a quiet signature scene. A 'Mrs. E. Morganroth' (spelling as printed) was on the 1920 Mountaineers outing.

place_names.name: Sol Duc (Soleduck) River and Hot Springs
place_names.origin_own_words: Early maps counted the river as part of the Quillayute. By 1923 the springs were 'Sol Duc' and the river 'Soleduck'; both spellings survive today. The hot-springs company told Meany that Native people found the springs first and that the name means 'magic waters'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Sol Duc, a river in the south western part of Clallam County, and hot-springs at which was developed a resort with hotel and postoffice. On early maps it was counted a part of Quillayute River. (Map by the Surveyor General of Washington Territory, 1857, in United States Public Documents, Serial Number 877.) More recently the hot-springs are called Sol Duc and the river Soleduck. (Henry Landes, A Geographic Dictionary of Washington, page 260.) The river is shown to be a branch, which, with the Bogachiel, forms the Quillayute River. The Sol Duc Hot Springs Company say the Indians were first to locate the springs and that the name means “magic waters.” (In Names MSS. Letter 452.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: 'Magic waters' is a resort company's claim (a sales line). Ask the Quileute Tribe before giving any meaning for Sol Duc.

place_names.name: Quillayute River, La Push, James Island
place_names.origin_own_words: Quillayute is the name of the Quileute people; the spelling was fixed by the U.S. Geographic Board. Meany (from Eells) says La Push is Chinook Jargon for 'mouth', from French 'la bouche'. Meany says James Island honors 'Chief Jimmy'; the Quileute Tribe's own site gives the island's Quileute name, A-Ka-Lat, 'Top of the Rock'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: La Push, a town at the mouth of the Quillayute River, in the southwestern part of Clallam County. It is a Chinook Jargon word meaning “mouth,” and originated in the French la boos. (Rev. Myron Eells, in American Anthropologist, January, 1892.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: La Push is the Quileute Tribe's village. The Tribe publishes visitor etiquette and a photography, video and sketching policy for tribal land; any illustrated scene set in La Push should be cleared with the Tribe. Use A-Ka-Lat only with the Tribe's agreement.

place_names.name: Mora
place_names.origin_own_words: The settlers' post office was first called Boston; mail for Boston, Massachusetts kept arriving, so postmaster Kron O. Erickson renamed it (by 1898) for his home parish of Mora in Sweden.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Mora, a postoffice at the mouth of the Quillayute River in the southwestern part of Clallam County. Mr. and Mrs. Frank T. Balch named the place Boston but so many letters for Boston, Massachusetts, were sent to the little office near the Pacific Ocean that K. O. Erickson, the next postmaster, had the new name substituted and thus honored his home town in Sweden. (Mrs. Frank T. Balch, in Names MSS., Letter 553.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Goodman Creek
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for a man on the 1890 township survey crew (per Isaac Anderson, postmaster at Hoh).

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Goodman Creek, a small creek emptying into the Pacific Ocean, western Jefferson County. It was named for a man working on the township survey in 1890. (Isaac Anderson of Hoh, in Names MSS., Letter 157.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Hoh River (Hoh Head, Hoh Peak, Hoh Lake)
place_names.origin_own_words: In 1787 Captain Barkley named the river 'Destruction River' after men from his ship were killed ashore; the name moved to the island and the river took the name of the Hoh people living at its mouth.
place_names.notes: The village of Hoh near the mouth later became Oil City (HRS ch. 2).

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Hoh River, a stream rising on Mount Olympus and flowing westward into the Pacific, in the northwestern part of Jefferson County. In 1787, the Indians killed a boat's crew sent for fresh water by Captain C. W. Barkley, who thereupon called it Destruction River. From similar experience at the same place Bodega y Quadra had named the nearby island Isla de Dolores. Barkley's name for the river was later transferred to the island, which is still known as Destruction Island. See paragraph under that head. The river then obtained the Indian name of Hoh, appearing in various forms such as Hooch, Holes, Huch, Hooh and Ohahlat. The Handbook of American Indians (Vol. I., p. 556) says it is the name of a band of Quilayute Indians, living at the river's mouth. The name is also used for a postoffice two miles up the river; for a promontory, Hoh Head, two and a half miles north of the mouth of the river; and a mountain, Hoh Peak, five and a half miles west of Mount Olympus.
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meany tells the 1775 and 1787 killings only from the ships' side and calls the Hoh 'a band of Quilayute Indians'. The Hoh Tribe is a sovereign nation; its own site gives its name as Chalá·at, 'People of the Hoh River'. Any scene at the river mouth needs review by the Hoh Tribe and Quileute Tribe.

place_names.name: Destruction Island
place_names.origin_own_words: Spanish sailors were killed ashore in 1775 and Bodega y Quadra named the island 'Isla de Dolores' (Island of Sorrows); Barkley's 1787 'Destruction River' name later passed to the island. Gilman (1896) adds that Hoh people kept potato patches on the island and used it as a lookout for whales; a first-order lighthouse stood there by 1896.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Destruction Island, in the Pacific Ocean, off the west shore of Jefferson County. On July 14, 1775, the Spanish Captain Bodega y Quadra sent a small boat's crew ashore for wood and water. Indians murdered the men and stole the boat. The captain called the island “Isla de Dolores,” or “Island of Sorrows.” In 1787, Captain Barkley, in the Austrian East India Company's ship Imperial Eagle, had a similar experience in the nearby river, which he named “Destruction River.” Later the Indian name of Hoh River was used but the word “Destruction” was passed on to the island. As early as April, 1792, Captain George Vancouver refers to Captain Barkley's Destruction Island.
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meany's words ('murdered', 'stole') are the sailors' one-sided version from 1923. Do not print this entry in the game as-is; paraphrase neutrally and have the Hoh and Quileute tribes review it.

place_names.name: Kalaloch
place_names.origin_own_words: An 1897 source spells the creek 'Klalops'. Settlers Samuel Castile and Tom Lawder lived at Kalaloch Cove by the late 1890s; Castile ran a post office there from 1903. Becker's resort (from the 1920s) became Kalaloch Lodge after the Park Service bought it in 1978.
place_names.indigenous_caution: Popular sources give a Quinault meaning for Kalaloch; we did not find it on a tribal site. Ask the Quinault Indian Nation before using any meaning.

place_names.name: Ozette (Lake, River, village) and Cape Alava
place_names.origin_own_words: Ozette is named in the 1855 Makah treaty; Ozette was one of the five permanent Makah villages. Coast-survey charts called the lake 'Lake of the Sun', which James Swan dismissed in 1887. Cape Alava carries a Spanish name from Manuel Quimper's 1790 chart ('Boca de Alava').

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Ozette, the name of a lake and a town on its shores, a creek, an island and an Indian Reservation, all near the Pacific Ocean, in the western part of Clallam County. The name is mentioned in the treaty by Governor Isaac I. Stevens with the Makahs, January 31, 1855. In an address at Port Townsend in 1887, Judge James G. Swan said: “There is a lake five or six miles inland from Hozett village at Flattery Rocks, which is marked on the coast survey charts ‘Lake of the Sun.’ The Makah name is Ka’houk, meaning a large body of fresh water, or simply lake. The sun part is imagination.” (Transactions of the Washington Pioneer Association, 1883-1889, pages 100-101).
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Ozette village and its excavated houses are Makah heritage (Makah Cultural and Research Center, Neah Bay). The Makah word in Swan's sentence should not be used in the game without Makah approval. Do not depict the village site, burials or artifacts.

place_names.name: Neah Bay and the Makah
place_names.origin_own_words: The Spanish named the bay Nunez Gaona and briefly fortified it in 1792. The present name, given by Kellett in 1847, comes (per Eells) from the name of the Makah leader Dee-ah, as pronounced by the Klallam. 'Makah' was a name given by neighbors; the Makah Tribe's site says it means 'people generous with food', while Meany (from Eells) gives 'cape people'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Neah Bay, a harbor near the entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca in the northeastern part of Clallam County. On August 15, 1788, Captain Charles Duncan, the British trader, indicated a bay at that place on his chart but did not give it a name. In 1790, the Spanish Captains Eliza and Quimper took possession and named the place “Bahia de Nunez Gaona” in honor of Haro y Peralta, a distinguished Spanish prelate, archbishop of Mexico in 1772 and viceroy from May 8 to August 16, 1787. In 1792 the Spanish Lieutenant Salvador Fidalgo was sent there to fortify the place. That work was abandoned the same year. Fragments of Spanish brick are still found in the banks of Neah Creek. Vancouver in that same year, 1792, charted the bay but did not stop there. (Edmond S. Meany, Vancouver's Discovery of Puget Sound, page 307, note.) American Traders called it “Poverty Cove” though the same is true of San Juan Harbor on the northern shore of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The Wilkes Expedition, 1841, made an elaborate map, calling it “Scarborough Harbour” in honor of Captain James Scarborough of the Hudson's Bay Company, who had rendered assistance to the Wilkes party. (J. G. Kohl, in Pacific Railroad Reports, Volume XII., Part I., pages 276-277.) The Wilkes chart made the first use of the word Neah but applied it to the islands now known as Waaddah. (United States Exploring Expedition, Hydrography, Volume XXIII., Atlas, chart 80.) The present name of the bay was given by Captain Henry Kellett in 1847. He spelled it Neeah Bay. (British Admiralty Chart 1911, Kellett, 1847.) The name comes from that of the Makah Chief Dee-ah. The Clallams, on the east, having a nasal language, called it Neah. (Rev. Myron Eells, in American Anthropoligist, January, 1892.)
meany_1923_verbatim.verification: page_image_checked for p. 184; last two sentences (p. 185) from archive.org OCR
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Where Meany and the Makah Tribe disagree on what 'Makah' means, the game should follow the Tribe. Shi Shi and Neah Bay are on the Makah Reservation; a Makah Recreation Pass is required (see coast.json).

place_names.name: Flattery Rocks
place_names.origin_own_words: Cook named Cape Flattery in 1778; Vancouver in 1792 put 'Flattery Rocks' on the rocks south of the cape where he thought Cook might have meant.
place_names.notes: The Flattery Rocks National Wildlife Refuge (1907) protects the offshore rocks; see coast.json.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Flattery Rocks, on the western coast of Clallam County south of Cape Flattery. The name arose through efforts of explorers to locate the place which Captain James Cook had named Cape Flattery. Vancouver in 1792 definitely located the name where it is now used and also recorded his effort at accuracy by charting the name Flattery Rocks where he thought it possible that Cook had intended to fix the name of Cape Flattery. Both names have remained where Vancouver placed them. See also Cape Alava and Cape Flattery.
meany_1923_verbatim.verification: page_image_checked (first lines); end from archive.org OCR
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Quinault (Lake, River, Indian Nation)
place_names.origin_own_words: The name of the Quinault people, first used for the tribe and then for the lake and river; the spelling was standardized by the U.S. Geographic Board. Lake Quinault's waters have been part of the Quinault Indian Reservation since before 1900.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Quinault, a lake, river and Indian Reservation in the northwestern part of Grays Harbor County. On the shore of the lake there is a postoffice with the same name. It was as the name of an Indian tribe that the name was first used. The Bureau of American Ethnology has collected an extensive synonymy. (Handbook of American Indians, Volume I., pages 342-343.) The present form, Quinault, has been approved by the United States Geographic Board. (Fifth Report 1890 to 1920, page 267.) The United States Coast and Geodetic Survey is now using the same form. (Chart 6002, corrected to June 25, 1921.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: The lake is managed by the Quinault Indian Nation (fishing and boating rules are the Nation's). In 2023 the Nation proposed the name Noskeliikuu for a creek in the North Fork Quinault area to replace an offensive name (WA State Register 23-05-046); the game must never use the old name.

place_names.name: Enchanted Valley
place_names.origin_own_words: Locally called the 'Valley of a Thousand Waterfalls'; Forest Service recreation planner F. W. Cleator suggested the name 'Enchanted Valley' to the Olson brothers, who built the chalet (completed August 1931).

place_names.name: Dodwell-Rixon Pass
place_names.origin_own_words: Named in July 1907 by the Parker-Browne-Clark party (guided by Will Humes) for Arthur Dodwell and Theodore F. Rixon, whose USGS survey crews mapped the forest reserve in 1898-1900. The same party named Humes Glacier on the east side of Olympus for their guide.

wood.locator: misc. item (e): note on Humes Ranch placard
wood.covers: Wood's correction that the Explorers Club party, not The Mountaineers, named Humes Glacier

place_names.name: Dodger Point
place_names.origin_own_words: The lookout (and by extension the point) is named for 'Dodger' Bender, the first lookout to staff the 1933 building, according to the 1982 NPS inventory card in the National Register nomination.

place_names.name: Ludden Peak
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for 'Doc' A. Ludden, a retired Tacoma policeman who from about 1906 to 1927 kept a beekeeping homestead and roadhouse ('Geyser Valley House and Apiary') half a mile below Humes Ranch.

place_names.name: Humes Ranch
place_names.origin_own_words: The cabin (about 1900) of Will and Grant Humes, brothers from a New York Adirondack guiding family who packed for hunters, climbers and The Mountaineers.

place_names.name: Krause Bottom
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for Ernst Krause (a German-born painter from Tacoma) and his wife Meta, who homesteaded here in the 1890s until a runaway slash fire burned their buildings and animals.

place_names.name: Michael's Cabin
place_names.origin_own_words: Built about 1937 by E. O. Michael ('Cougar Mike', a bounty hunter, trapper and packer) with Jay Gormley and Gus Peterson.

place_names.name: Remann's Cabin (Elk Lick Lodge)
place_names.origin_own_words: Fishing cabin of Frederick G. Remann (Tacoma lawyer, Pierce County superior court judge 1926-1948), built in the 1920s under Grant Humes's supervision; he called it Elk Lick Cabin. About 1939 the river's change of course forced it to be taken apart and rebuilt on the higher shelf where it stands.

place_names.name: Camp Wilder and the Botten (Wilder) cabin
place_names.origin_own_words: The nearby patrol cabin is H. H. Botten's 1920s fishing cabin (Botten Cabin, also called Wilder Patrol Cabin). Botten was one of the four Bremerton climbers who reached all three Olympus summits in one day in 1908. 'Wilder' follows Mount Wilder, a Press Expedition name (see press_expedition.json).

place_names.name: Elkhorn (Elwha)
place_names.origin_own_words: Already 'Elkhorn Flat, between the Lillian and the Lost rivers' when The Mountaineers planned their third camp there in 1907; the Forest Service built the guard station in 1930-34. (The 1920 outing's 'Elkhorn camp' was a different spot on the Dosewallips.)

place_names.name: Chicago Camp
place_names.origin_own_words: Already called 'Chicago Camp, ten miles below the source of the Elwha' when Grant Humes used it as headquarters in August 1905. A 1900 scientific party from Chicago's Field Columbian Museum worked in the Elwha; the camp may be named for it, but no source we read says so.

place_names.name: Olympic Hot Springs (Boulder Creek)
place_names.origin_own_words: Reported by Andrew Jacobsen in the early 1890s; rediscovered by William (Billy) Everett about 1907 and opened to the public in 1909 as Olympic Hot Springs.

place_names.name: Heart O' the Hills
place_names.origin_own_words: Taken from a small private resort (store, gas station, cabins) on the north flank of Mount Angeles from the late 1920s; Claude Spencer ran it near Lake Dawn in the 1940s.

place_names.name: Spruce (Hoh post office)
place_names.origin_own_words: The post office John Huelsdonk kept in his home on the upper Hoh (1904 for 29 years), named for the spruce timber around it. The site is about two miles outside the park's west boundary.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Spruce, a postoffice on the Hoh River in the western part of Jefferson County, so named on June 18, 1904, because of a local predominance of spruce timber. (John Huelsdonk, in Names MSS. Letter 171.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Lake Cushman and Staircase
place_names.origin_own_words: Lake Cushman honors the man Meany calls Orvington Cushman ('Devil Cush'), packer and interpreter for Gov. Isaac Stevens at the 1854-55 treaties (other sources spell the first name 'Orrington'; not checked here). Staircase took its name from the resort (1930s-1950s) at the road's end; we have not confirmed in our sources the often-told story that the name goes back to a 'staircase' route built by O'Neil's men in 1890.
place_names.confidence: high for Lake Cushman; low for the Staircase origin story

wood.covers: settlers and Wright's hunting lean-to found by the O'Neil party near Lake Cushman and Five Stream, 1890

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Lake Cushman, in the Olympic Mountains, west of Hood Canal, Mason County. It was named in honor of Orvington Cushman, packer and interpreter with Governor Isaac I. Stevens when the treaties with the Indians were being made. Cushman advocated putting all the Indians on one big reservation on Hood Canal. He was known as “Devil Cush.” A postoffice at the lake was established on June 6, 1893. The lake has long been famous as a resort. (W. Putnam, in Names MSS., Letter 75.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Cushman's plan to put all Native people on one reservation is part of treaty-era history that hurt the Skokomish (Twana) and others. Do not celebrate the namesake; consult the Skokomish Indian Tribe for any Staircase scene.

place_names.name: Mount Gladys and Gladys Divide (Skokomish)
place_names.origin_own_words: A party of campers named Mount Gladys in summer 1913 for Gladys Easterbrook, daughter of Army chaplain Edmund P. Easterbrook; Gladys Divide lies beside it. (Gladys Lake in Grand Valley is a different place.)

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Mount Gladys, near Lake Cushman, Mason County. Elevation, 5,700 feet. It was named by a company of campers in the summer of 1913, in honor of Gladys, daughter of Chaplain Edmund P. Easterbrook, of the United States Army. (Seattle Post-Intelligencer, August 17, 1913.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Skokomish River
place_names.origin_own_words: The Wilkes Expedition charted it as 'Black Creek' in 1841. Meany (from Eells) says the Native name means 'river people'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Skokomish River, rising in the Olympic mountains and flowing into Hood Canal at Union, in the northwestern part of Mason County, was named “Black Creek” by the Wilkes Exploring Expedition, 1841. (Narrative, Volume IV, page 411) This was probably intended as an honor for the trader Black at one of the northern posts. Captain Wilkes wrote: “To Mr. Black the world is indebted for the greater part of the geographical knowledge which has been published of the country west of the Rocky Mountains.” (Narrative, Volume IV, page 369.) That name did not persist. The present Indian name means “river people”, from kaw, “fresh water” and mish, “people”, (Myron Eells in American Anthropologist for January, 1892.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Ask the Skokomish Indian Tribe (Twana) before using any meaning or Twana word.

place_names.name: Mount Constance (Lake Constance, Constance Pass) and The Brothers
place_names.origin_own_words: George Davidson of the U.S. Coast Survey named the high peaks seen from Puget Sound in 1856 for the Fauntleroy family: Mount Constance for Constance Fauntleroy, Mount Ellinor for Ellinor Fauntleroy (later his wife) and The Brothers for Arthur and Edward Fauntleroy.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Mount Constance, above Hood Canal, in the east central part of Jefferson County. Elevation, 7,777 feet. (United States Geological Survey, Dictionary of Altitudes, page 1015.) Captain George Davidson of the United States Coast Survey named it in 1856 for Constance Fauntleroy, later Mrs. James Runcie. She was a woman of much talent in literature and music. She died in Illinois on May 17, 1911, aged 75 years. (Edmond S. Meany: The Story of Three Olympic Peaks, in the Washington Historical Quarterly, Volume IV., pages 182-186.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Dosewallips River
place_names.origin_own_words: Meany has no entry for the river itself. The Wilkes Expedition (1841) called the sandspit at its mouth Sylopash Point, and Kellett in 1847 applied that name to the river; it did not last. The 1894 prospectors spelled it 'Docewallups'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Sylopash Point, a large sandspit at the mouth of the Dosewallips River, in the eastern part of Jefferson County, so named by the Wilkes Expedition, 1841. (Hydrography Volume XXIII, Atlas, chart 78.) In 1847, Captain Henry Kellett extended the name to apply to the Dosewallips River. (British Admiralty Chart 1911.) The name has not persisted.

place_names.name: Duckabush River
place_names.origin_own_words: Meany (from Eells, 1892) derives it from a Native word for 'a reddish face', after a reddish bluff or mountain near the mouth.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Duckabush River, flowing into Hood Canal near the town of the same name. Rev. Myron Eells (American Anthropologist, January, 1892), says the name is derived from the Indian word do-hi-a-boos, meaning “a reddish face.” The bluff or mountain near the place has a reddish appearance.
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Twana-language claim from a missionary; check with the Skokomish Indian Tribe.

place_names.name: Quilcene
place_names.origin_own_words: From the name of a Twana band that lived on Quilcene Bay ('salt-water people', per Eells).

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Quilcene, a bay, the northwestern projection of Dabop Bay, in the eastern part of Jefferson County. A town on the bay bears the same name. The word has been spelled “Colcene”, “Colseed”, “Quilceed”. Rev. Myron Eells, for many years a missionary among the Hood Canal Indians, says: “Quil-ceed is a Twana name, from quil-ceed-o-bish, the name of a band of Twanas who lived on Quilceed bay. It means ‘salt-water people’, in distinction from the S-kaw-kaw-bish, or ‘fresh-water people’, another band of the same tribe.” (American Anthropoligist, for January, 1892.) Quilcene is the form on most recent charts including No. 6450 of the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey.
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Twana words; consult the Skokomish Indian Tribe.

place_names.name: Dungeness
place_names.origin_own_words: Vancouver (April 1792) named the low sand spit New Dungeness after Dungeness on the English Channel; the name spread to the river and town.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Dungeness, a town, harbor and river on the shore of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, in Clallam County. In April, 1792, Captain George Vancouver wrote: “The low sandy point of land, which from its great resemblance to Dungeness in the British channel, I called New Dungeness * * * ” (Voyage Around the World, second edition, Volume II., page 55.) That name, thus applied first to the point or spit, has been extended to other uses.
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.name: Sequim
place_names.origin_own_words: From the name of a Klallam village on Washington Harbor (Meany, from Eells); a pioneer told Meany it meant 'quiet water'.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Sequim, a town in the northwestern part of Clallam County. Rev. Myron Eells says the Clallam tribe had a village on Washington Harbor, just south of New Dungeness Bay and the village was known in the Clallam language as Such-e-kwai-ing, from which has been derived the word Sequim. (American Authopologist for January, 1892, and Handbook of American Indians, Volume II., page 510.) Matthew Fleming, a pioneer who lived in that vicinity for more than sixty years, thinks the present word is as near as we can get to a proper spelling of the Clallam word, meaning “quiet water.” The Indians applied it to Washington Harbor but the white people have extended it to the prairie and the town. (J. H. McCourt, postmaster at Sequim, in Names MSS. Letter 572.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: This is Jamestown S'Klallam homeland (the Tribe's offices are at Blyn near Sequim). Confirm any Klallam word or meaning with the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe.

place_names.name: Wynoochee
place_names.origin_own_words: Gannett (via Meany) says the river was named for its shifting course.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Wynoochee River, a tributary of the Chehalis River at Montesano, in the east central part of Grays Harbor County, was so named because of its varying course. The name is an Indian word meaning “shifting.” (Henry Gannett, Origin of Certain Place Names in the United States, page 331.) George Gibbs referred to the stream by its present name on March 1, 1854. (Pacific Railroad Reports, Volume I., page 468.)
meany_1923_verbatim.public_domain_reason: Published in the United States in 1923 (before 1931).

place_names.indigenous_caution: Meaning from a non-Native gazetteer; check with the Quinault Indian Nation or other tribes of the Chehalis basin before use.

place_names.origin_own_words: Named for William Gladstone Steel of Portland, founder of the Oregon Alpine Club, which co-sponsored O'Neil's 1890 expedition. Meany only knew Gannett's one-line entry.

meany_1923_verbatim.verbatim_entry: Steel, “a mountain in Washington named for William G. Steel, of Portland, Oregon.” (Henry Gannett, Origin of Certain Place Names in the United States, page 290.) The location is not given.

place_names.name: Mount Fromme, Mount Claywood, Lost Pass, Hayden Pass country
place_names.origin_own_words: On the 1920 Mountaineers outing a party that climbed Mount Claywood went on to a peak about a mile northwest and named it Mount Fromme for Rudo L. Fromme, supervisor of Olympic National Forest, who was with them. Bailey's account already uses the names Hayden Pass, Service Pass and Mount Sentinel, and mentions 'the pass leading to Lost Creek' (today's Lost Pass). The origin of 'Hayden' is not given in our sources.

place_names.name: Kestner Homestead and Kestner Creek
place_names.origin_own_words: Anton (Antone) and Josepha Kestner, Austrian immigrants; Anton took up the claim in 1891, the family lost its first house to a flood, and the second house dates from about 1900-1905. Nearby Merriman Falls and Gatton Creek also carry settlers' names.

place_names.name: Ahlstrom's Prairie (and Roose's Prairie)
place_names.origin_own_words: Swedish-born homesteaders Lars Ahlstrom and Peter Roose (born Arvard Hammerlund) took adjoining claims on the open prairies about 1.5 miles west of Lake Ozette after the area reopened to homesteading around 1900; they kept sheep and gardens and took outside work for cash.

place_names.name: Oil City
place_names.origin_own_words: The village of Hoh near the river mouth (post office 1904, Isaac Anderson postmaster) later took the name Oil City from oil prospecting on the west slope.

place_names.name: Norwegian Memorial and Chilean Memorial
place_names.origin_own_words: Grave memorials to shipwrecked sailors: the Norwegian bark Prince Arthur (night of 2 January 1903; 18 of 20 crew died; monument erected 1904 by Seattle's Norse Club) and the schooner-barge W. J. Pirrie, wrecked near Cape Johnson in a November 1920 gale (most aboard died, including the captain's wife and child, by most accounts).
place_names.notes: Real graves. Treat with respect: no jokes, no looting, no ghosts. The Pirrie details vary between sources (see uncertain_claims).

place_names.name: Forks
place_names.origin_own_words: Settlers' 'Forks Prairie' lies between the Calawah and Bogachiel rivers near the Sol Duc, which join to form the Quillayute. HistoryLink reports the name was picked partly because 'Ford's Prairie' was already taken elsewhere in Washington, and that the prairie has Quileute names meaning roughly 'prairie upstream'. The Pullen family were among the first homesteaders on Quillayute Prairie nearby.
place_names.indigenous_caution: Ask the Quileute Tribe before using the Quileute names for the prairie.

place_names.name: Brinnon
place_names.origin_own_words: Named for E. P. Brinnon (first name given as Ewell or Elwell), who took a donation land claim near the river mouths on Hood Canal about 1858-1860. The post office opened in 1891 under his name after 'Dosewallips' was judged too hard to spell. The 1920 Mountaineers outing started here.

place_names.name: Klahhane Ridge
place_names.origin_own_words: From the Chinook Jargon word usually spelled klahanie, 'out, outdoors'. A Port Angeles hiking club, the Klahhane Club, was active by World War I (its 'Klahhane annual' was published in 1918) and had its clubhouse at Lake Dawn near Heart O' the Hills. Whether the club named the ridge is not confirmed.

indigenous.principle: The country O'Neil crossed is the homeland of the Skokomish (Twana) people on the Hood Canal side and the Quinault on the Quinault River side; the 1885 route lies in Klallam country (today the Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam and Port Gamble S'Klallam tribes). The Park Service names eight tribes with ties to the park: Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, Port Gamble S'Klallam, Skokomish, Quinault, Hoh, Quileute and Makah.
rules: The Olympic Peninsula is the homeland of the Makah, Quileute, Hoh, Quinault, Klallam (Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, Port Gamble S'Klallam) and Skokomish (Twana) peoples, among others. The Park Service lists eight tribes with a continuing relationship to the park.

Record facts only, from tribal or authoritative sources. Do not retell sacred or traditional stories, do not reconstruct legends (including the legend chapters of Wood's The Land That Slept Late), and do not invent names, speech or scenes.

Say 'first recorded' or 'first documented', never 'first ever'. Frame 1890s 'unknown land' talk as a newcomer's view; old blazes, hide posts, trails and village sites in the explorers' own reports show long Native use of the mountains.
Do not print Native-language place-name meanings from old books (Meany, Eells) as fact. None in this file has been confirmed by a tribe.
Do not quote period remarks about Native people from O'Neil, Henderson or Meany; several are offensive and some are wrong.
Every card with flags.consult_before_use names the nation to write to before that card ships. Write to the nation, follow its answer, and record the answer here.

notes.note: The Press route starts in the homeland of the Klallam (S'Klallam) people on the lower Elwha, today the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, a sovereign, federally recognized nation that has lived there since time immemorial and signed the 1855 Treaty of Point No Point. It ends in Quinault country: Lake Quinault, the lower Quinault River and the Quinault Indian Agency at Taholah, today the Quinault Indian Nation.

The 1889-90 Press framed the interior as never trodden by anyone, 'white or Indian'. NPS says Native Americans had long known the interior. The party's own report contradicts the myth: very old blazes healed into trees (one with about 210 rings over the cut), old hide-working posts, old trails, and a bench Barnes took for a long-abandoned village site (MTN1907). The game should not repeat 'first to see' or 'unexplored' claims except as quoted 1890 attitudes, clearly framed.

A modern columnist reports a Klallam elk-hunting camp near today's park boundary (Christie dismissed the hunters as knowing nothing of the country) and a night in an abandoned Klallam house near the later Glines Canyon dam site. At the end, two Quinault men in a canoe were with the settler Antrim when he found the starving party, and Quinault country carried them by canoe to the coast. Do not invent names, speech or scenes for these people.

The 1890 list explains 'Elwha' as an Indian name meaning elk. Do not present that, or the origin of 'Queets' or 'Quinault', as settled fact in game text without checking with the tribes. The Klallam and Quinault have their own names for these places; the game should ask before using any of them.

notes.topic: The Elwha dams and the river today
notes.note: The Elwha and Glines Canyon dams (built in the early 1900s) blocked salmon and flooded Klallam homelands and cultural sites; their removal began September 17, 2011 and finished in 2014. Our glines_canyon_overlook node stands on the old dam. Any story beat there should credit the tribe's long campaign and avoid describing cultural sites.

Before using any Indigenous content tied to this route (the Semple Plateau 'village site', the old blazes, the hunting camp, the abandoned house, the canoe rescue, place-name meanings), contact the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe (elwha.org, info@elwha.org, 360-452-8471) and the Quinault Indian Nation (Taholah, 360-276-8211). Do not retell sacred stories. Recorded here as facts only, with no cultural interpretation.
1885: a Native guide left O'Neil's party on its first night out of Port Angeles (Wood, COL1990 p.41); Evans also notes a Native guide and packer who joined later. Neither is named.
1890: O'Neil hired Native packers at times to carry supplies on schedule (SDOC59 p.3). They are not named.
1890: Pvt. Fisher, alone on the lower Queets, was helped by Native people (Wood, COL1990 p.45).
1890: a Quinault household sheltered and fed O'Neil for a night on the Quinault River (SDOC59 p.16), and the agency at Taholah gave him dry clothes and dinner.

O'Neil wrote that the rivers carry names given by the peoples living at their mouths, and he collected name translations and 'legends'; those appendices were not printed in 1896 and we have not seen them.

The NPS lists eight tribes with a continuing relationship to Olympic National Park: Lower Elwha Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, Port Gamble S'Klallam, Skokomish, Quinault, Hoh, Quileute and Makah. Their ancestors ceded lands and waters by treaties in 1855 and 1856 and kept rights to fish, hunt and gather in 'usual and accustomed places'; a 1974 federal court decision (U.S. v. Washington) upheld treaty fishing rights. The park and the eight treaty tribes signed a memorandum of understanding to work together.

notes.topic: Makah (Neah Bay, Shi Shi, Ozette, Cape Alava)
notes.note: The Makah Tribe says it has lived at Neah Bay since time immemorial, had five permanent villages (Waatch, Sooes, Deah, Ozette, Bahaada) and signed the Treaty of Neah Bay on 31 January 1855, reserving whaling, sealing and fishing rights. The Makah Cultural and Research Center in Neah Bay holds material from ancestors recovered at Ozette in the 1970s. A Makah Recreation Pass is required for visitors.
notes.do_not: Do not depict the Ozette village site, burials, artifacts, whaling ceremonies or the Wedding Rocks petroglyphs' meanings without Makah approval. Do not use Makah words.

notes.topic: Quileute (La Push, Rialto, Second and Third Beach)
notes.note: The Quileute Tribe says its homeland reached from the Pacific beaches up the rain-forest rivers to the glaciers of Mount Olympus, that the Quileute language is not known to be related to any other, and that its people signed the Treaty of Quinault River (1855) and the Treaty of Olympia (1856). A one-square-mile reservation at La Push was set aside on 22 February 1889; that year a settler burned all 26 houses in the village. The Tribe publishes 'Indian Country Etiquette' and a photography, video and sketching policy for tribal land.
notes.do_not: Do not retell Quileute stories (the Tribe's site lists stories and family-owned songs and dances); do not draw La Push or Quileute people without the Tribe's permission.

notes.note: The Hoh Tribe calls itself Chalá·at, 'People of the Hoh River', lives on the Hoh Indian Reservation at the river's mouth and ties that move to the Quinault Treaty of 1 July 1855. Old non-Native sources (Meany 1923) treat the Hoh as a 'band' of another tribe; the game should treat the Hoh Tribe as the sovereign nation it is.
notes.do_not: Do not retell the 1775/1787 'Destruction' killings from the ships' side only.

notes.topic: Quinault (Lake Quinault, the Quinault and Queets rivers)
notes.note: Lake Quinault's waters were included in the Quinault Indian Reservation before 1900 and the Nation sets lake rules. Quinault canoe people carried early explorers (the Gilmans in 1889, the Press party in 1890, the 1920 Mountaineers to Taholah); their names are not recorded in our sources. In 2023 the Nation proposed 'Noskeliikuu' to replace an offensive creek name in the North Fork Quinault area.

notes.topic: Klallam / S'Klallam (Elwha, Port Angeles, Sequim, Dungeness)
notes.note: The Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe's homeland includes the Elwha valley; the dams flooded its homelands and cultural sites, and the Tribe led the long effort for their removal (completed 2014). The Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe ('The Strong People') traces its community to 210 acres bought for $500 in gold in 1874 under Lord James Balch, and won federal recognition on 10 February 1981; Meany's 'Chief James' of Jamestown is the same leader. The Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe is the third S'Klallam nation.

The Skokomish Indian Tribe's mission is to preserve 'the traditional values, and treaty rights of the Twana people'. Many east-side names (Quilcene, Duckabush, Dosewallips, Skokomish) are Twana words recorded by a missionary; their meanings in Meany should not be printed without the Tribe's review.

1890s-1900s writers (Landes 1907, Collier's 1909, the Press, Meany's 'discovered') called the interior unknown or unexplored. That was true only for newcomers. Old blazes, trails and village sites met by the explorers, and the tribes' own histories, show long Native use of the mountains. Quote those lines only as period attitudes and frame them.

Some period sources in this file use terms now considered offensive (a Chinook Jargon word for women used in place names, and a Jargon phrase for a Native home in the 1920 article). None of these are quoted. The game should use current tribal names and current official place names only.

Before shipping any Indigenous name, meaning, story, image or site in the game, write to the tribe concerned and follow its answer: Makah (makah.com), Quileute (quileutetribe.com), Hoh (hohtribe-nsn.org), Quinault Indian Nation (360-276-8211), Lower Elwha Klallam (elwha.org, 360-452-8471), Jamestown S'Klallam (jamestowntribe.org), Port Gamble S'Klallam (pgst.nsn.us), Skokomish (skokomish.org, 360-426-4232). The NPS Ethnographic Overview (Wray 1997) is useful background but does not replace consultation.
